# onecheck

> Simple, scriptable health checks for a server: YAML rules, cron, exit codes, result files and an event queue.

# onecheck
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck

Simple, scriptable health checks for a server. You describe checks in YAML,
cron (or a systemd timer) runs `onecheck`, and onecheck tells you what is
broken: by exit code, on stdout (text or JSON), in per-rule result files, and
through an event queue that records every pass → fail and fail → pass change.

```console
$ onecheck -c /etc/onecheck/config.yaml
PASS   passwd-sane   (file, 2ms)
FAIL   api-health    (http, 124ms)  [transition: fail]
       body json status: expected equals "ok", got "degraded"
PASS   nginx-active  (command, 9ms)

3 rules: 2 passed, 1 failed, 0 errors
$ echo $?
1
```

## How it works

- **Modules collect, onecheck decides.** A check type (`file`, `http`,
  `command`, `disk`, `systemd`, `cpu`, `memory`, `docker`, `ports`, ...) is a
  separate executable, `onecheck-<name>`, living in a modules directory. A
  module only returns values (status code, file size, stdout, ...). All
  comparisons are done by one engine inside onecheck, so every operator works
  the same for every module.
- **Modules are picked up dynamically.** onecheck looks into the modules
  directory on every run. Install a module and the next run can use it.
- **State is tracked for you.** For every rule onecheck remembers the
  confirmed state and how many runs in a row passed or failed. With
  `fail_after: 3` a rule must fail three times in a row before it is
  considered failed. Each confirmed change is written as a JSON event for a
  notification service to pick up.
- **Notifications are a separate tool.** [onenotify](https://alekzonder.github.io/onenotify)
  takes the events and sends them to Telegram, mail or ntfy.

## Quick start

```sh
# 1. install the latest onecheck and the bundled modules
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alekzonder/onecheck/main/install.sh | sh

# 2. write a config
mkdir -p /etc/onecheck && cat > /etc/onecheck/config.yaml <<'YAML'
name: main
rules:
  - name: site-up
    module: http
    params: { url: https://example.com/ }
    check:
      status: 200
      body: { contains: "Example Domain" }
YAML

# 3. check the config, then run it
onecheck validate
onecheck
```

[Getting started](/getting-started) walks through installation, the first
config and scheduling with cron or systemd.

| | |
|---|---|

| [State and events](/state-and-events) | `fail_after` / `pass_after`, the event queue contract |

| [Development](/development) | build, test, release |

`onecheck --help` and `onecheck <command> --help` describe every command and
flag. The source is on [GitHub](https://github.com/alekzonder/onecheck).

# Checks
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/checks

The `check` block of a rule says what must be true about the values a module
returned. It is evaluated by onecheck itself, by one engine, so everything on
this page works the same for every module: bundled or third-party.

```yaml
rules:
  - name: api-health
    module: http
    params: { url: https://example.com/health }
    check:
      status: 200                                  # field: condition
      headers.content-type: { contains: json }     # path into a field
      body:
        json:
          assert:
            - { path: status, equals: ok }
```

A rule **passes** when every condition holds. Each condition that does not
hold is reported separately, with what was expected and what was found:

```
body json status: expected equals "ok", got "degraded"
```

A rule without `check` passes whenever its module could collect the data.

## Paths

Each key of `check` is a path to a value. The first part is a field of the
module (see the module's page for its fields); further parts go into objects
and arrays:

| Path | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status` | the field `status` |
| `headers.content-type` | key `content-type` of the object field `headers` |
| `items.0` | first element of an array |
| `items.#` | number of elements of an array |

Paths use [GJSON path syntax](https://github.com/tidwall/gjson/blob/master/SYNTAX.md).
A key that itself contains a dot is written with a backslash: `headers.x\.y`.

A field that does not exist for the module is a config error, caught by
`onecheck validate`.

## Conditions

A condition is one of:

- **a plain value** — shorthand for `equals`:

  ```yaml
  status: 200          # same as  status: { equals: 200 }
  exists: true
  ```

- **a mapping of operators** — all of them must hold:

  ```yaml
  size: { gt: 0, lt: 10MB }
  ```

- **a combinator** — `all`, `any`, `not`, described [below](#combining-conditions).

To compare with an object, use `equals` explicitly, because a bare mapping is
read as operators.

## Operators

| Operator | Applies to | Holds when |
|---|---|---|
| [`equals`](#equals-not_equals) / `not_equals` | anything | the value is (not) exactly this |
| [`contains`](#contains-not_contains) / `not_contains` | string, array, object | substring / element / key is (not) present |
| [`starts_with`](#starts_with-ends_with) / `ends_with` | string | the string starts / ends with this |
| [`matches`](#matches-not_matches) / `not_matches` | string | the regular expression matches (does not match) |
| [`glob`](#glob-not_glob) / `not_glob` | string | the whole string matches (does not match) a shell pattern |
| [`gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`](#gt-gte-lt-lte) | number | greater / greater-or-equal / less / less-or-equal |
| [`in`](#in-not_in) / `not_in` | anything | the value is (not) one of the list |
| [`exists`](#exists) | anything | the path is present (`true`) or absent (`false`) |
| [`type`](#type) | anything | the value has this JSON type |
| [`length`](#length) | string, array, object | a nested condition holds for the length |
| [`every`](#every-some) / `some` | array | a nested condition holds for each / at least one element |
| [`path`](#path) | anything | the other operators apply to a value inside this one |
| [`json`](#json) | string | the string is JSON and satisfies `assert` / `schema` |

An operator applied to a value of the wrong type (for example `gt` on a
string) does not hold, and the message says which type was found. An unknown
operator or a malformed argument is a config error.

### `equals`, `not_equals`

Exact comparison of JSON values. There is no conversion between types: the
number `200` is not equal to the string `"200"`.

```yaml
status: { equals: 200 }
mode: { equals: "0644" }           # quote it: mode is a string
exists: { equals: true }
headers.x-env: { not_equals: staging }
tags: { equals: [a, b] }           # arrays and objects compare as a whole
```

### `contains`, `not_contains`

```yaml
body: { contains: "status: ok" }       # string: substring
stdout: { not_contains: ERROR }
roles: { contains: admin }             # array: has an element equal to this
headers: { contains: x-request-id }    # object: has this key
```

### `starts_with`, `ends_with`

```yaml
headers.content-type: { starts_with: application/json }
target: { ends_with: .conf }
```

### `matches`, `not_matches`

Regular expressions in [Go RE2 syntax](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp/syntax). The
expression may match anywhere in the string; anchor it with `^` and `$` for a
full match.

```yaml
stdout: { matches: 'version \d+\.\d+' }
body: { not_matches: '(?i)exception|traceback' }     # (?i): ignore case
```

Command output usually ends with a newline, and `$` only matches at the very
end of the text. Use the multi-line flag `(?m)` to let `^` and `$` match at
line boundaries:

```yaml
stdout: { matches: '(?m)^active$' }
```

Write regular expressions in single quotes so YAML leaves backslashes alone.

### `glob`, `not_glob`

Shell patterns, matched against the **whole** string, case-sensitive:

| Pattern | Matches |
|---|---|
| `*` | any run of characters, including `/` and none at all |
| `?` | exactly one character |
| `[abc]`, `[a-z]` | one character from the set or range |
| `[!abc]` | one character not in the set |

Everything else is literal: `.` is a dot, `+` is a plus.

```yaml
image: { glob: "registry.local/*" }      # any image from this registry
name: { not_glob: "tmp-*" }
```

Quote patterns that start with `*` or `[`: YAML reads those characters
specially.

### `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`

Numeric comparison.

```yaml
status: { gte: 200, lt: 300 }
exit_code: { lte: 1 }
```

Fields that hold a size or a time span accept literals with units. The
module's page marks such fields as **bytes** or **duration**:

```yaml
size: { lt: 10MB }             # B, KB, MB, GB, TB (1024-based)
age: { lt: 1h }                # ms, s, m, h, d, w; also 1h30m
duration: { lte: 500ms }
tls_expires_in: { gt: 14d }
```

Unit literals work for `equals`, `not_equals`, `in`, `not_in` too, and only
directly on such a field (not on values inside JSON).

A module that returns a list can mark keys of its elements as **bytes** or
**duration** as well. A literal then works wherever a condition addresses
that key of one element:

```yaml
filesystems: { every: { path: free, gt: 5GB } }       # under every / some
filesystems.0.free: { gt: 5GB }                        # by index
filesystems.#(mountpoint=="/").free: { gt: 5GB }       # first match of a query
filesystems.#(fstype=="ext4")#:                        # a filtered list
  every: { path: free, gt: 5GB }
```

It does not work on a list of values (`filesystems.#.free`) or on a key the
module's page does not mark.

### `in`, `not_in`

```yaml
status: { in: [200, 204, 304] }
type: { not_in: [symlink, other] }
```

### `exists`

Whether the path is present at all. Use it for optional keys and for the
absence of something:

```yaml
headers.strict-transport-security: { exists: true }
headers.x-debug-token: { exists: false }
```

`exists` is the only operator that can hold for an absent path; see
[Missing values](#missing-values).

> The `file` module also has a *field* named `exists` (does the file exist).
> `check: { exists: true }` compares that field; it is the plain-value
> shorthand, not this operator.

### `type`

One of `string`, `number`, `bool`, `object`, `array`, `null`.

```yaml
headers: { type: object }
body:
  json:
    assert:
      - { path: items, type: array }
      - { path: deleted_at, type: "null" }     # quote null
```

### `length`

Applies a nested condition to the length of a string (in characters), an
array (elements) or an object (keys). A plain number means `equals`.

```yaml
stdout: { length: { gt: 0 } }          # not empty
body: { length: { lte: 4096 } }
items: { length: 3 }
```

### `every`, `some`

Apply a condition to the elements of an array. The argument is a condition;
a list of conditions means all of them.

```yaml
containers:
  every:                                   # each element must satisfy all
    - { path: state, equals: running }
    - { path: restart_count, lt: 5 }
tags: { some: { glob: "env-*" } }          # at least one element
```

| | holds when | empty array |
|---|---|---|
| `every` | the condition holds for each element | holds |
| `some` | the condition holds for at least one element | does not hold |

A value that is not an array, or a missing path, does not hold.

`every` reports each failing element separately, with its index in the
path. For an element that is an object the message also shows its simple
keys (strings, numbers, booleans; nested objects such as labels are left
out), so you see which element it was:

```
containers.2.state: expected equals "running", got "exited" (element {"id":"3f2a…","name":"old","state":"exited",...})
containers.#(state=="running")#.1: expected any [...], got {"id":"9c1e…","image":"xmrig/xmrig","name":"miner",...}
```

The index counts elements of the array the condition is applied to; after a
query such as `#(state=="running")#` that is the filtered array.

`some` reports one failure with the whole array.

Combine with a [GJSON query](#paths) to pick elements first, for example only
running containers:

```yaml
containers.#(state=="running")#:
  every:
    any:
      - { path: name,  in: [nginx, postgres] }
      - { path: image, glob: "registry.local/*" }
```

A query that matches nothing gives an empty array: `every` holds, `some`
does not.

### `path`

Inside any condition mapping, `path` moves the other operators of that
mapping to a value inside the current one. It is how conditions reach the
fields of array elements:

```yaml
containers.0: { path: state, equals: running }   # same as containers.0.state: running
```

`path` uses the same [GJSON syntax](#paths) as check keys and needs at least
one operator next to it. A missing sub-path is handled like any
[missing value](#missing-values). Unit literals (`10MB`, `1h`) apply under
`path` only when it names a key of an element that the module marks as
**bytes** or **duration**, see [above](#gt-gte-lt-lte); otherwise compare
with plain numbers.

### `json`

Parses a string field as JSON and checks the document. It works on any string
field: an HTTP `body`, a command's `stdout`, a file's `content`. A string that
is not valid JSON does not hold.

```yaml
body:
  json:
    assert:      # optional: list of path + operators
      - { path: status, equals: ok }
    schema:      # optional: a JSON Schema
      type: object
      required: [status]
```

At least one of `assert` and `schema` is required; both may be used together.

#### `json.assert`

A list of assertions. Each has a `path` into the parsed document and any of
the operators above (several operators on one line are ANDed):

```yaml
body:
  json:
    assert:
      - { path: status, equals: ok }
      - { path: version, matches: '^2\.' }
      - { path: data.items, type: array }
      - { path: data.items.#, gte: 1 }                   # at least one item
      - { path: data.items.0.id, type: number }
      - { path: data.user.email, exists: true }
      - { path: error, exists: false }
      - { path: 'data.items.#(state=="failed")#', length: 0 }   # no failed items
      - { path: 'data.items.#.name', contains: primary }        # some item is named primary
      - path: latency_ms
        any:
          - { lt: 100 }
          - { equals: null }
```

Paths are [GJSON paths](https://github.com/tidwall/gjson/blob/master/SYNTAX.md):

| Path | Selects |
|---|---|
| `a.b.c` | nested keys |
| `items.0` | array element by index |
| `items.#` | number of elements |
| `items.#.name` | the `name` of every element, as an array |
| `items.#(state=="ok")` | first element whose `state` is `ok` |
| `items.#(state=="ok")#` | all such elements, as an array |
| `items.#(size>100)#.name` | names of all elements with `size` over 100 |

#### `json.schema`

A [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) (draft 2020-12) written in YAML.
Use it when the *shape* of the document matters: required keys, types,
enumerations, formats of nested objects.

```yaml
body:
  json:
    schema:
      type: object
      required: [status, checks]
      properties:
        status: { enum: [ok, degraded] }
        checks:
          type: array
          minItems: 1
          items:
            type: object
            required: [name, state]
            properties:
              state: { enum: [ok] }
```

Every schema violation becomes its own failure, with the location inside the
document:

```
body json /checks/1/state: schema violation: value must be 'ok'
```

`assert` is shorter for "this key has this value"; `schema` is better for
structure. They combine freely.

## Combining conditions

Operators written side by side are ANDed. For other logic use combinators;
they nest to any depth.

```yaml
# any: at least one must hold
status:
  any:
    - { equals: 200 }
    - { equals: 304 }

# all: every one must hold (same as writing the operators side by side,
# but allows the same operator twice)
body:
  all:
    - { contains: "db: ok" }
    - { contains: "cache: ok" }

# not: must not hold
stdout:
  not: { matches: '(?i)error|fatal' }

# nested
body:
  any:
    - { contains: "status: ok" }
    - all:
        - { contains: "status: degraded" }
        - not: { contains: "db: down" }
```

When `any` does not hold, one failure is reported for the whole `any`.

## Missing values

A path can be absent: an optional header, a key that is not in the JSON, a
field the module does not return in this situation (the `file` module returns
no `size` for a file that does not exist).

For an absent path **every operator fails**, including the negative ones
(`not_equals`, `not_contains`, `not_matches`, `not_in`) and `not: {...}`. The
only exceptions are `exists: false` and a `not` around `exists`. The message
says `got nothing (path is missing)`.

The reason: missing data must never make a check pass by accident. If an API
stops returning the key you are watching, the check fails instead of going
quiet. When absence is acceptable, say so explicitly:

```yaml
- path: error
  any:
    - { exists: false }
    - { equals: null }
```

An explicit JSON `null` is a present value: `exists: true` holds, and so does
`type: "null"`.

## Large values

A module returns at most `run.max_field_size` (default `10MB`) per field.
When a condition uses a field that had to be cut, the rule ends with the
status `error` rather than passing or failing on partial data. Raise the
limit, or check something smaller (a file's `size` instead of its `content`).

## Recipes

```yaml
# a file exists, is not empty, and is fresh
check:
  exists: true
  size: { gt: 0 }
  age: { lt: 25h }

# a file must NOT exist
check:
  exists: false

# a JSON config file has a value
check:
  content:
    json:
      assert:
        - { path: db.host, equals: localhost }

# HTTP: status, header, body substring, response time
check:
  status: { in: [200, 204] }
  headers.content-type: { starts_with: application/json }
  body: { contains: '"healthy":true' }
  duration: { lt: 1s }

# TLS certificate valid for at least two more weeks
check:
  tls_expires_in: { gt: 14d }

# command: exit code and a number parsed from output
check:
  exit_code: 0
  stdout:
    json:
      assert:
        - { path: queue.length, lt: 1000 }

# command output has no error lines and is not empty
check:
  stdout:
    length: { gt: 0 }
    not_matches: '(?im)^error'
```

---

# Configuration
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/configuration

The config is YAML. Unknown keys are errors, so a typo never goes unnoticed.
Check a config without running it: `onecheck validate -c <file>`.

## Full reference

```yaml
name: main                    # REQUIRED. [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.-]*

log:
  level: info                 # debug | info | warn | error
  dir: /var/log/onecheck      # log file: <dir>/<name>/onecheck.log
  format: text                # text | json
  rotate:                     # rules for "onecheck logrotate"
    max_size: 10MB            # rotate when the log is larger
    keep: 5                   # rotated files to keep
    max_age: 30d              # remove rotated files older than this
    compress: true            # gzip rotated files

paths:
  modules: /usr/lib/onecheck/modules   # where onecheck-<name> executables live
  results: /var/lib/onecheck/results   # results go to <results>/<name>/
  events:  /var/lib/onecheck/events    # event queue, shared by all configs
  state:   /var/lib/onecheck/state     # state goes to <state>/<name>/

include:                      # more rule files (globs)
  - conf.d/*.yaml

events:
  ttl: 24h                    # lifetime of an event in the queue

run:
  parallel: 4                 # checks running at the same time
  max_field_size: 10MB        # largest single value a module may return

defaults:                     # used by rules that do not set the key
  timeout: 30s
  fail_after: 1
  pass_after: 1
  output_tail: 10k            # how much module output is kept in a result
  event_params: true          # events carry the rule's params; false hides a rule's details
  remind_every: 60m           # a rule that stays failed writes a reminder event this often; 0 = never

modules:
  repos:                      # default repositories for "onecheck module search"
    - alekzonder/onecheck

rules:
  - name: api-health          # REQUIRED, unique. [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.-]*
    module: http              # REQUIRED. module name: [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*
    enabled: true             # false: the rule is skipped
    tags: [api, web]          # for "onecheck run --tag"
    timeout: 10s              # the module is killed after this
    fail_after: 3             # consecutive failures before state "fail"
    pass_after: 2             # consecutive passes before state "pass" again
    output_tail: 1k           # output kept in the result; 0 keeps none
    event_params: true        # false: no params in events, events marked "redacted"
    event_output: [body]      # output fields a notification may show; default: none
    remind_every: 60m         # reminder events while the state stays "fail"; 0 = never
    params:                   # input of the module, see docs/modules/
      url: https://example.com/health
    check:                    # conditions, see docs/checks.md
      status: 200
```

Every key except `name` is optional; the values above are the defaults for
root. Sizes accept `B`, `KB`, `MB`, `GB`, `TB` (1024-based); durations accept
`ms`, `s`, `m`, `h`, `d`, `w` and combinations such as `1h30m`.

`remind_every` is described in [State and events](/state-and-events#reminders),
`event_output` in [State and events](/state-and-events#output-in-notifications).

## `name`

The name is required and keeps configs on the same host apart:

- results: `<paths.results>/<name>/<rule>.json`
- state and run lock: `<paths.state>/<name>/`
- log: `<log.dir>/<name>/onecheck.log`

Rule names only have to be unique within one config. The event queue
(`paths.events`) is shared by all configs; every event carries the config
name.

Two different config files must not use the same name: onecheck remembers
which file owns a name and refuses to run the second one (exit code `2`).
If you move or rename a config file and keep its name, delete
`<paths.state>/<name>/.owner` once; the next run records the new location.

## Default paths

| | root | other users |
|---|---|---|
| `log.dir` | `/var/log/onecheck` | `$HOME/.local/state/onecheck/log` |
| `paths.modules` | `/usr/lib/onecheck/modules` | `$HOME/.local/lib/onecheck/modules` |
| `paths.results` | `/var/lib/onecheck/results` | `$HOME/.local/state/onecheck/results` |
| `paths.events` | `/var/lib/onecheck/events` | `$HOME/.local/state/onecheck/events` |
| `paths.state` | `/var/lib/onecheck/state` | `$HOME/.local/state/onecheck/state` |

Relative paths in the config are resolved against the directory of the config
file.

onecheck creates these directories with mode `0750` and the files in them
(results, state, events, logs) with mode `0640`. Results and events can
contain pieces of what was checked, such as file content or command output,
so they are not readable by everyone. To let another service read results or
events, put its user into the group owning the directories.

## Where everything is: `onecheck paths`

`onecheck paths` prints the full path of everything onecheck reads and writes
for the config it would use, so the paths do not have to be worked out from
the tables above:

```
$ onecheck paths
config    /etc/onecheck/config.yaml  (from default location)
name      main
include   /etc/onecheck/conf.d/api.yaml
include   /etc/onecheck/conf.d/db.yaml
log       /var/log/onecheck/main/onecheck.log
state     /var/lib/onecheck/state/main
results   /var/lib/onecheck/results/main
events    /var/lib/onecheck/events  (missing)
modules   /usr/lib/onecheck/modules
binary    /usr/local/lib/onecheck/versions/0.1.2/onecheck
```

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `config` | the config file and how it was found: `--config`, `ONECHECK_CONFIG` or `default location` |
| `name` | the config's `name`; it is part of the log, state and results paths |
| `include` | every include file that was read, in reading order |
| `log` | the log file, see [Logging and logrotate](/logging-and-logrotate) |
| `state` | the confirmed state of each rule, see [State and events](/state-and-events#files) |
| `results` | the latest result of each rule |
| `events` | the event queue, shared by all configs on the host |
| `modules` | where modules are looked for |
| `binary` | the onecheck executable itself, with symlinks resolved |

`(missing)` marks a path that does not exist yet. The log, state, results and
events paths are created by the first run, so they are missing on a fresh
install.

The command changes nothing, does not need the modules to be installed and
works with rules that are broken. If the config file is found but cannot be
loaded, its path is still printed, followed by the error, and the exit code
is `2`.

`onecheck paths --json` prints the same for scripts:

```json
{
  "name": "main",
  "config": { "path": "/etc/onecheck/config.yaml", "exists": true, "source": "default location" },
  "includes": [
    { "path": "/etc/onecheck/conf.d/api.yaml", "exists": true }
  ],
  "log": { "path": "/var/log/onecheck/main/onecheck.log", "exists": true },
  "state": { "path": "/var/lib/onecheck/state/main", "exists": true },
  "results": { "path": "/var/lib/onecheck/results/main", "exists": true },
  "events": { "path": "/var/lib/onecheck/events", "exists": false },
  "modules": { "path": "/usr/lib/onecheck/modules", "exists": true },
  "binary": { "path": "/usr/local/lib/onecheck/versions/0.1.2/onecheck", "exists": true }
}
```

## Includes (`conf.d/`)

```yaml
include:
  - conf.d/*.yaml
  - /etc/onecheck/team-*/rules.yaml
```

- Patterns are globs; relative ones are resolved against the config file's
  directory. A pattern that matches nothing is fine.
- Files are read in lexicographic order, after the rules of the main file.
- An include file may contain only the `rules` key:

  ```yaml
  # conf.d/web.yaml
  rules:
    - name: site-up
      module: http
      params: { url: https://example.com/ }
      check: { status: 200 }
  ```

- A rule name used twice, in any files, is an error naming both files.

## Environment variables in `params`

Strings inside `params` may reference environment variables as `${VAR}`,
which keeps secrets out of the config file:

```yaml
params:
  url: https://api.example.com/health
  headers:
    Authorization: "Bearer ${API_TOKEN}"
```

- Only the `${VAR}` form is expanded. A plain `$VAR` is left alone, so shell
  commands in the `command` module keep working.
- Write `$${VAR}` to get a literal `${VAR}`. Every other `$` (including the
  shell's `$$`, `$1`, `$(...)`) is passed through unchanged.
- An undefined variable makes that rule an error; it is never replaced by an
  empty string.
- `check` is never expanded.
- Events carry `params` as written here, with `${VAR}` not replaced, so a
  secret passed this way does not reach a notification. A secret written into
  the config as plain text does. `event_params: false` on a rule (or in
  `defaults`) keeps the params out of its events altogether, see
  [State and events](/state-and-events#what-an-event-can-reveal).

## Logging level

The level comes from, in order: `--log-level`, `log.level`, `info`.

## Two kinds of config errors

**Errors of the whole config** stop onecheck with exit code `2` before any
check runs: unreadable or invalid YAML, an unknown top-level key, a missing or
invalid `name`, a rule without a name, a duplicate rule name, an include file
with keys other than `rules`.

**Errors of a single rule** make only that rule unusable. On `onecheck run`
the rule gets the status `error` with the reason, and every other rule still
runs. This covers: an unknown key in the rule, an invalid rule name, a missing
`module`, a module that is not installed or not compatible, `params` the
module does not accept, a condition on a field the module does not have, an
unknown operator or a bad operator argument, an undefined `${VAR}`.

Such an `error` counts as a failure for the rule's state, so after
`fail_after` runs it produces a `fail` event: a broken rule is reported
through the same channel as a broken service, instead of silently
disappearing. The keys of the rule that could be read still apply to that
event: a rule with a misspelt key and `event_params: false` stays hidden, and
`remind_every` is honoured. A rule that cannot be checked allows no output
to be shown, whatever its `event_output` says.

`onecheck validate` prints all errors of both kinds and exits with `2` if
there are any.

---

# Development
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/development

Rules for contributors (commit messages, merges, limits) are in
[AGENTS.md](https://github.com/alekzonder/onecheck/blob/main/AGENTS.md). This page is about how to build, test and release.

## Requirements

- Go (the version in `go.mod` or newer)
- `make`
- network access the first time `make lint` runs: it installs a pinned
  `golangci-lint` into `./bin`
- for the documentation site only: Node.js 22 and npm

## Make targets

| Target | What it does |
|---|---|
| `make build` | builds `dist/onecheck` and `dist/modules/onecheck-{file,http,command,disk,systemd,cpu,memory,docker,ports}` |
| `make test` | `go test -race ./...` |
| `make fmt` | formats the code with `gofmt` |
| `make lint` | `golangci-lint`, including cyclomatic complexity |
| `make check` | `fmt-check` + `go vet` + `lint` + `test`; **must pass before a change is done** |
| `make release-assets` | cross-builds release assets and `checksums.txt` into `dist/release/` |
| `make docs-build` | checks documentation links and builds the site into `docs/dist/` |
| `make docs` | builds the site and publishes it to branch `docs` |
| `make clean` | removes `dist/` |

Builds are static (`CGO_ENABLED=0`). The version is injected with
`make build VERSION=1.2.3`; without it the version is `dev`.

A new bundled module is picked up by the Makefile automatically: every
directory `cmd/onecheck-<name>` is built as a module.

## Cyclomatic complexity

`gocyclo` runs as part of `make lint` with a limit of **25** per function
(`.golangci.yml`). It applies to tests too. When a function goes over the
limit, split it; do not raise the limit and do not silence the linter.

## Layout

```
cmd/onecheck/              core CLI entrypoint
cmd/onecheck-file/         bundled modules: main.go (description),
cmd/onecheck-http/           collect.go (data collection)
cmd/onecheck-command/
pkg/module/                public SDK for module authors: protocol types, Main
internal/match/            the matching engine: compile + evaluate "check"
internal/config/           find, load, include, ${VAR} expansion, defaults
internal/modules/          find modules, describe, run a module process
internal/state/            pass/fail state machine (pure logic)
internal/store/            atomic files, run lock, state/result/event files
internal/result/           Result and Event JSON contracts
internal/runner/           validate rules, execute, record
internal/output/           text and JSON rendering, exit code
internal/logging/          slog setup
internal/rotate/           logrotate: logs and expired events
internal/github/           GitHub Releases client
internal/install/          module install/update/remove, self-update
internal/cli/              cobra commands
internal/testmods/         builds bundled modules for tests
examples/                  example config, validated by a test
docs/                      user documentation, built into the site by Blume
scripts/                   documentation link check and publishing
```

How a run flows through the packages:

```
cli.run
 └─ config.Find / config.Load
 └─ runner.Run
     ├─ store.Open, Lock
     ├─ per rule: prepare        modules.Describe, params schema, match.Compile
     ├─ per rule: modules.Check  starts onecheck-<module>, reads field values
     │            match.Eval     conditions → failures
     └─ per rule: state.Advance → store.WriteEvent → SaveState → WriteResult
 └─ output.Write, output.ExitCode
```

## Design rules

- **Modules collect, the core decides.** Never put comparison logic into a
  module. A new way of comparing is a new operator in `internal/match`,
  where it immediately works for all modules.
- **One failing rule never stops the others.** Anything wrong with a single
  rule becomes that rule's `error` result. Only problems of the whole config
  or of onecheck's own files end a run with exit code `2`.
- **No lost transitions.** For each rule the event is written before the
  state. Keep that order.
- **Atomic files.** Everything under results, state and events is written
  with `store.WriteFileAtomic`.
- **The protocol is a contract.** Changing the JSON exchanged with modules
  incompatibly requires a new `module.ProtocolVersion` and a range in
  `internal/modules` that still accepts the old one.

## Tests

- Unit tests sit next to the code. The matching engine and the state machine
  are table-driven.
- Tests that need real modules build them once per package through
  `internal/testmods` (`runner`, `cli`). `internal/modules` uses a fake
  module from `testdata/fakemod` that can misbehave on purpose.
- Module management is tested against an in-memory GitHub client
  (`internal/install`) and against a local HTTP server speaking the GitHub
  API shape (`internal/github`, `internal/cli`).
- `examples/config.yaml` (with its `conf.d/` includes) is loaded and
  validated against all bundled modules by `TestExamplesLoadAndValidate`, so
  examples cannot drift from the code. The test also fails when a bundled
  module (`cmd/onecheck-<name>`) has no example rule: a new module comes with
  an example.
- Tests must not use the network and must not write outside `t.TempDir()`.

Run one package or one test:

```sh
go test ./internal/match
go test ./internal/runner -run TestRunTransitionWritesEvent -v
```

## Adding an operator

1. Add a table-driven case (passing and failing) to
   `internal/match/match_test.go`, and a case to `TestCompileErrors` for bad
   arguments.
2. Implement it in `internal/match/ops.go` and register it in `leafOps`.
3. Document it in `docs/checks.md`.

## Adding a bundled module

1. Create `cmd/onecheck-<name>/` with `main.go` (description, params schema,
   fields) and `collect.go`, following the existing modules.
2. Test `collect` directly; include `TestDescriptionCoversFields`.
3. Add `docs/modules/<name>.md` (with `title` and `sidebar.label`
   frontmatter like the other module pages), list it in
   `docs/modules/meta.ts` and link it from `README.md` and `docs/index.md`.

## Releasing

Releases are built by GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) when a
tag `vX.Y.Z` is pushed:

```sh
git tag v1.2.0
git push origin v1.2.0
```

The workflow runs `make check`, then `make release-assets VERSION=1.2.0` and
publishes a GitHub release with:

```
onecheck_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-file_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-http_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-command_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-disk_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-systemd_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-cpu_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-memory_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-docker_<os>_<arch>
onecheck-ports_<os>_<arch>
checksums.txt
```

for linux and darwin on amd64 and arm64. These names are what
`onecheck module install` and `onecheck self-update` look for.

After the release is published, the workflow's `docs` job runs `make docs`,
which publishes the documentation of the tagged commit (see
[Documentation site](#documentation-site)).

Environment overrides useful when testing update flows against a fork:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ONECHECK_GITHUB_API` | API base URL instead of `https://api.github.com` |
| `ONECHECK_SELF_UPDATE_REPO` | repository `self-update` downloads from |
| `ONECHECK_SELF_UPDATE_TARGET` | path of the binary `self-update` replaces |

## Documentation site

The pages under `docs/` are published at <https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck>
by [Blume](https://useblume.dev). `docs/` is the Blume project and its own
content root:

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `docs/blume.config.ts` | site settings: base `/onecheck`, excluded folders |
| `docs/package.json`, `docs/package-lock.json` | the pinned Blume version |
| `docs/index.md` | the home page |
| `docs/meta.ts`, `docs/modules/meta.ts` | sidebar order |
| `docs/public/` | static files served at the site root |

Every `.md` page under `docs/` is published, except `docs/superpowers/`
(internal designs and plans) and build folders. To keep a new folder off the
site, add it to `content.exclude` in `docs/blume.config.ts`.

**Links between pages use site routes, never `.md` paths:**
`[Checks](/checks#gt-gte-lt-lte)`, `[disk](/modules/disk)`. Blume prefixes
the base `/onecheck` itself; it does not rewrite relative `.md` links, so they
would break on the site. `scripts/docs-check-links.sh` fails the build when one
appears. Links from outside the site (README, CLI messages) use the full URL
`https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/<route>`.

**A page's title goes in the front matter, never in a `# ` heading:**

```markdown
---
title: Getting started
---

## Install
```

Blume renders the title above the page itself, so a `# Getting started`
line would show it a second time. Sections start at `##`. The same script
fails the build on a `# ` line outside code blocks.

Preview locally with `cd docs && npm ci && npm run dev`.
`make docs-build` runs the link check, `blume doctor` and `blume build`; CI
runs it on every push and pull request (`.github/workflows/check.yml`).

`make docs` (`scripts/publish-docs.sh`) builds the site and commits
`docs/dist` to branch `docs`, creating it on first use. GitHub Pages serves
branch `docs`, path `/`. The release workflow runs it for every tag, so the
site always shows the latest release.

---

# Getting started
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/getting-started

## Install

onecheck is one static binary plus one executable per check module.

### With the install script

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alekzonder/onecheck/main/install.sh | sh
```

The script detects the system and CPU, asks GitHub for the latest release,
verifies the download against the release's `checksums.txt`, and installs
onecheck together with the bundled modules (`file`, `http`, `command`, `disk`, `systemd`, `cpu`, `memory`, `docker`, `ports`) of the
same version.

A specific version:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alekzonder/onecheck/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --version 0.1.0
```

Every version gets its own directory, and a symlink in a bin directory points
at the chosen one:

| | Linux | macOS |
|---|---|---|
| versions | `/usr/local/lib/onecheck/versions/<version>/onecheck` | `~/.local/share/onecheck/versions/<version>/onecheck` |
| symlink | `/usr/local/bin/onecheck` | `~/.local/bin/onecheck` |
| modules | `/usr/lib/onecheck/modules` | `~/.local/lib/onecheck/modules` |

On Linux the install is system-wide, and the script calls `sudo` when it is
not run as root. On macOS everything stays in the home directory; if
`~/.local/bin` is not in `PATH`, the script says how to add it.

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `--version <v>` | version to install (`0.1.0` or `v0.1.0`); default: the latest release. Also `ONECHECK_VERSION` |
| `--root <dir>` | where versions are kept |
| `--bin-dir <dir>` | where the `onecheck` symlink is created |
| `--modules-dir <dir>` | where the bundled modules go |
| `--no-modules` | install onecheck only |

Set `GITHUB_TOKEN` if GitHub's rate limit gets in the way.

To upgrade, downgrade or switch back, run the script again. A version that is
already on disk is not downloaded again, only the symlink is switched, and the
modules are brought to the same version. Old versions are kept until you
delete their directories under `versions/`. `onecheck self-update` refuses to
touch a binary installed this way, because it would overwrite one version's
directory with another version.

The modules directories above are the defaults of `paths.modules`: the Linux
one for root, the macOS one for a regular user. If you run onecheck on Linux
as a regular user, set `paths.modules: /usr/lib/onecheck/modules` in the
config, or install with `--modules-dir ~/.local/lib/onecheck/modules`.

### By hand

1. Download `onecheck_<os>_<arch>` from the
   [releases](https://github.com/alekzonder/onecheck/releases), verify it
   against `checksums.txt`, and put it into `PATH` as `onecheck`:

   ```sh
   install -m 0755 onecheck_linux_amd64 /usr/local/bin/onecheck
   onecheck version
   ```

2. Install the bundled modules (`file`, `http`, `command`, `disk`, `systemd`, `cpu`, `memory`, `docker`, `ports`):

   ```sh
   onecheck module install alekzonder/onecheck --modules-dir /usr/lib/onecheck/modules
   onecheck module list --modules-dir /usr/lib/onecheck/modules
   ```

   Once a config exists, `--modules-dir` is not needed: the directory is
   taken from `paths.modules`.

Or build everything from source: `make build` puts the binary into
`dist/onecheck` and the modules into `dist/modules/`.

## First config

onecheck looks for its config in this order:

1. `--config <path>` (`-c`)
2. `$ONECHECK_CONFIG`
3. `/etc/onecheck/config.yaml`
4. `$HOME/.config/onecheck/config.yaml`

A minimal config needs a name and some rules:

```yaml
name: main

rules:
  - name: root-disk-marker
    module: file
    params:
      path: /etc/hostname
    check:
      exists: true
      size: { gt: 0 }

  - name: site-up
    module: http
    params:
      url: https://example.com/
    check:
      status: 200
```

Each rule has three parts:

- `module` — which module collects the data;
- `params` — the module's input (what to look at);
- `check` — conditions on the values the module returns.

See [examples/config.yaml](../examples/config.yaml) for a fuller example,
[Configuration](/configuration) for every key and [Checks](/checks)
for everything `check` can express.

## Validate and run

```sh
onecheck validate          # reports every config problem at once, runs nothing
onecheck paths             # where the config, log, state, results and events are
onecheck                   # run all rules; same as "onecheck run"
onecheck --only-failed     # print only what is wrong
onecheck -o json           # machine-readable output
onecheck --rule site-up    # run one rule
```

The exit code is `0` when every rule passed, `1` when something failed, `2`
when onecheck could not run at all. Details: [Output and results](/output-and-results).

## Schedule it

onecheck has no scheduler of its own. Run it from cron:

```cron
# /etc/cron.d/onecheck
* * * * *   root  onecheck --only-failed >/dev/null
17 3 * * *  root  onecheck logrotate >/dev/null
```

or from a systemd timer:

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/onecheck.service
[Unit]
Description=onecheck run

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/onecheck --only-failed
# exit code 1 means "a check failed", which is not a unit failure
SuccessExitStatus=1
```

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/onecheck.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run onecheck every minute

[Timer]
OnCalendar=minutely
AccuracySec=5s

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

### Checks at different intervals

Use one config per interval, each with its own `name`, and one schedule line
per config:

```cron
* * * * *    root  onecheck -c /etc/onecheck/fast.yaml --only-failed >/dev/null
*/15 * * * * root  onecheck -c /etc/onecheck/slow.yaml --only-failed >/dev/null
```

Configs with different names never block each other: results, state, logs and
the run lock are kept per name. If a run of the *same* config is still in
progress when the next one starts, the new one exits with code `2`.

## What gets written where

With the default paths, for root:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| latest result of each rule | `/var/lib/onecheck/results/<name>/<rule>.json` |
| state between runs | `/var/lib/onecheck/state/<name>/` |
| events (pass ↔ fail changes) | `/var/lib/onecheck/events/` |
| log | `/var/log/onecheck/<name>/onecheck.log` |
| modules | `/usr/lib/onecheck/modules/` |

For other users everything lives under `$HOME/.local/state/onecheck/` and
`$HOME/.local/lib/onecheck/modules/`. All of it is configurable:
[Configuration](/configuration).

---

# Logging and logrotate
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/logging-and-logrotate

## Log file

Every run appends to

```
<log.dir>/<config name>/onecheck.log
```

by default `/var/log/onecheck/<name>/onecheck.log` for root and
`$HOME/.local/state/onecheck/log/<name>/onecheck.log` for other users. The
directory is created when needed. `onecheck paths` prints the exact path for
the current config.

```yaml
log:
  level: info      # debug | info | warn | error
  dir: /var/log/onecheck
  format: text     # text | json
```

| Level | What is logged |
|---|---|
| `error` | a run that could not complete |
| `warn` | recoverable problems, e.g. an unreadable state file, a `remind_every` shorter than the time between runs |
| `info` | one line per rule with its outcome, state changes and reminders (`reminder written`), a summary per run |
| `debug` | additionally, per rule: the params and fields requested from the module, the values it returned (long strings cut to 256 bytes), the state counters; the modules found; what modules printed on their stderr |

The level is taken from `--log-level`, then `log.level`, then `info`:

```sh
onecheck --log-level debug --rule api-health
```

`text` format:

```
time=2026-11-23T10:00:00.123Z level=INFO msg="check failed" rule=api-health module=http status=fail state=pass duration_ms=124 failures="[status: expected equals 200, got 503]"
time=2026-11-23T10:00:00.130Z level=INFO msg="state changed" rule=api-health transition=fail event=20261123T100000Z-main-api-health-fail
time=2026-11-23T10:00:00.131Z level=INFO msg="run finished" total=12 passed=11 failed=1 errors=0
```

`json` format writes the same records as one JSON object per line.

Messages at `warn` and above are also printed on stderr, so cron mails them.
With `--log-level` on the command line, stderr shows everything at that level
as well, so a run can be watched in the terminal:

```sh
onecheck --log-level debug --rule api-health
```

`log.level` in the config changes only the log file, never stderr. Log lines
never go to stdout, which carries only results.

At `debug` the log contains rule params and returned values as they are,
including HTTP headers and command output. Do not leave `log.level: debug`
on if those hold secrets.

If the log file cannot be opened, onecheck prints a warning, logs to stderr
for that run, and still runs the checks.

## `onecheck logrotate`

onecheck does not depend on the system's logrotate. One command takes care of
both things that would otherwise grow forever: the log and the event queue.

```sh
onecheck logrotate            # logs and events
onecheck logrotate --logs     # only the log of this config
onecheck logrotate --events   # only expired events
```

Schedule it, for example once a day:

```cron
17 3 * * *  root  onecheck logrotate >/dev/null
```

With several configs, run it once per config (logs are per config):

```cron
17 3 * * *  root  onecheck logrotate -c /etc/onecheck/fast.yaml >/dev/null
18 3 * * *  root  onecheck logrotate -c /etc/onecheck/slow.yaml >/dev/null
```

### Logs

```yaml
log:
  rotate:
    max_size: 10MB   # rotate when the log is larger than this
    keep: 5          # number of rotated files to keep
    max_age: 30d     # also remove rotated files older than this
    compress: true   # gzip rotated files
```

When `onecheck.log` is larger than `max_size`:

- `onecheck.log` becomes `onecheck.log.1` (or `onecheck.log.1.gz`);
- existing `onecheck.log.N` move to `N+1`;
- the next run starts a new `onecheck.log`.

On every call, rotated files with an index above `keep`, or older than
`max_age`, are removed. The log is only rotated when it is too large, so
calling `logrotate` often is harmless.

Rotation takes the config's run lock. If a run is in progress at that moment
the logs are skipped with a message and handled by the next call.

### Events

```yaml
events:
  ttl: 24h
```

An event is written with `expires_at` = time of the event + `events.ttl`.
`onecheck logrotate` removes events whose `expires_at` has passed. This only
matters for events nobody consumed: a notification service normally deletes
events as it processes them (see [State and events](/state-and-events)).

The event queue is shared by all configs, so the cleanup of any one config
covers all of them. Each event keeps the lifetime it was written with.

Files in the queue directory that cannot be read as events, and temporary
files left by an interrupted write, are removed once they are older than
`events.ttl`.

---

# Module management
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/module-management

A module is an executable file named `onecheck-<name>` in the modules
directory (`paths.modules`). onecheck reads that directory on every run:
there is no registry to refresh and nothing to restart. A module is usable
from the moment its file is there, and gone when the file is removed.

Modules are distributed through GitHub Releases. The `onecheck module`
commands download, verify and install them; you can also copy a module file
into the directory by hand.

All commands take the modules directory from the config. Without a config,
pass `--modules-dir <dir>`.

## List

```console
$ onecheck module list
modules in /usr/lib/onecheck/modules:
NAME     VERSION  PROTOCOL  COMPATIBLE  SOURCE               DESCRIPTION
command  1.2.0    1         yes         alekzonder/onecheck  Run a command and return its exit code, stdout and stderr
file     1.2.0    1         yes         alekzonder/onecheck  Inspect a file, directory or symlink: ...
http     1.2.0    1         yes         alekzonder/onecheck  Make an HTTP/HTTPS request and return ...
```

`SOURCE` is the repository a module was installed from; `-` means the file
was put there by hand. `COMPATIBLE` says whether this onecheck can talk to
the module, see [Compatibility](#compatibility).

## Search

```sh
onecheck module search                         # repositories from modules.repos in the config
onecheck module search alekzonder/onecheck someone/onecheck-postgres
```

Lists every release of the repositories and the modules each release has for
this machine's OS and architecture, with the command to install each.

## Install

```sh
onecheck module install alekzonder/onecheck              # every module of the latest release
onecheck module install alekzonder/onecheck http         # one module, latest release
onecheck module install alekzonder/onecheck file@1.2.0   # a specific version
```

"Latest" is the newest release that is not marked as a pre-release. A
pre-release is only installed when asked for by version.

What install does, per module:

1. downloads the asset into a temporary file inside the modules directory;
2. compares its sha256 with the release's `checksums.txt` — a release without
   `checksums.txt`, or without an entry for the asset, is refused;
3. runs the downloaded file with `describe` and checks that it is the module
   it claims to be and speaks a supported protocol version;
4. renames it into place in one step, replacing a previous version;
5. records repository, version and checksum in `installed.json` in the
   modules directory.

If any step fails, nothing changes: a previously installed version keeps
working, and no partial file is left.

## Update

```sh
onecheck module update            # all modules installed with "module install"
onecheck module update http file  # only these
```

Each module is updated to the latest stable release of the repository it was
installed from. For every module onecheck prints either `updated <name> to
<version>` or `skipped <name>: <reason>`. Reasons include: already up to
date; the new release speaks a protocol this onecheck does not support
(update onecheck first); the module was copied in by hand, so its source is
unknown.

A skip is not a failure. An update that was attempted and failed (download
error, checksum mismatch, a module that does not run) stops the command with
exit code `2`; the installed version stays in place.

## Remove

```sh
onecheck module remove http
```

Rules that still use the module will get status `error` ("module is not
installed").

## Updating onecheck itself

```sh
onecheck self-update                  # latest stable release
onecheck self-update --version 1.4.0  # a specific one
```

The asset `onecheck_<os>_<arch>` is downloaded next to the running binary,
verified against `checksums.txt`, started once (`version`) to prove it runs,
and then renamed over the current binary in one step. On any failure the
current binary is left untouched. The user running the command needs write
access to the directory of the binary.

A onecheck installed with `install.sh` lives in a per-version directory and
is not updated by `self-update` (the command refuses): run `install.sh`
again, see [Getting started](/getting-started#with-the-install-script).

`self-update` does not touch modules, and `module update` does not touch
onecheck. A typical sequence:

```sh
onecheck self-update && onecheck module update
```

## Compatibility

onecheck and modules are versioned independently. What must match is the
**module protocol**: the JSON a module and onecheck exchange.

- Every module reports the protocol version it speaks.
- Every onecheck supports a range of protocol versions; `onecheck version`
  prints it.
- A module outside that range is shown as not compatible by `module list` and
  `validate`; rules using it get status `error`; `install` and `update`
  refuse to install such a version.

Module versions themselves (semver, the release tag without the leading `v`)
are only used to decide whether an update is available.

Bundled modules (`file`, `http`, `command`, `disk`, `systemd`, `cpu`, `memory`, `docker`, `ports`) are released together with
onecheck from the same repository and carry the same version number, but any
mix that shares a protocol version works.

## Repositories of third-party modules

Any GitHub repository can distribute modules. A release needs:

- one asset per module and platform, named
  `onecheck-<name>_<os>_<arch>`, e.g. `onecheck-postgres_linux_amd64`
  (`<os>` and `<arch>` as in Go: `linux`, `darwin`; `amd64`, `arm64`);
- an asset `checksums.txt` in `sha256sum` format covering them:

  ```
  3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855  onecheck-postgres_linux_amd64
  ```

Module names are lower-case letters, digits, `_` and `-`. See
[Module protocol](/module-protocol) for how to write a module.

Add repositories you use to the config so that `module search` covers them:

```yaml
modules:
  repos:
    - alekzonder/onecheck
    - someone/onecheck-postgres
```

## Environment

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | sent to the GitHub API: higher rate limits, access to private repositories |
| `ONECHECK_GITHUB_API` | API base URL instead of `https://api.github.com` (GitHub Enterprise) |

## Security notes

- Checksums come from the same release as the files. They protect against
  corrupted or truncated downloads, not against a compromised repository.
  Only install modules from repositories you trust: a module runs with the
  privileges of onecheck.
- Modules are looked up only in the modules directory, never in `PATH`. Keep
  that directory writable by root (or the onecheck user) only.

---

# Module protocol
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/module-protocol

This page is for people writing a module. A module teaches onecheck a new
kind of check: Postgres, Redis, DNS, a message queue, anything.

## The idea

A module is a standalone executable named `onecheck-<name>`. onecheck starts
it once per check, hands it the rule's `params` on stdin as JSON, and reads
**field values** from its stdout as JSON.

A module never decides whether a check passed. It returns facts ("status is
503", "the file is 2 KB"); onecheck evaluates the rule's `check` conditions
on them. That is why every operator, JSON assertions and JSON Schema work for
every module without the module doing anything.

A module can be written in any language. For Go there is a small SDK,
`github.com/alekzonder/onecheck/pkg/module`.

Protocol version described here: **1**.

## Invocations

A module must implement two subcommands.

### `onecheck-<name> describe`

Prints a JSON description on stdout and exits with `0`. It must be fast and
free of side effects: onecheck calls it on every run and on install.

```json
{
  "protocol": 1,
  "name": "redis",
  "version": "0.3.0",
  "description": "Ping a Redis server and read INFO",
  "params_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "required": ["addr"],
    "properties": {
      "addr": { "type": "string" },
      "password": { "type": "string" }
    }
  },
  "fields": {
    "ping":        { "type": "string",   "description": "reply to PING" },
    "role":        { "type": "string",   "description": "master or replica" },
    "used_memory": { "type": "bytes",    "description": "memory used by Redis" },
    "uptime":      { "type": "duration", "description": "time since start" },
    "info":        { "type": "object",   "description": "all INFO keys" }
  }
}
```

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `protocol` | yes | protocol version the module speaks |
| `name` | yes | module name; must equal `<name>` in the file name |
| `version` | yes | module version (semver) |
| `description` | no | one line, shown by `onecheck module list` |
| `params_schema` | no | JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for the rule's `params`; onecheck validates `params` with it before starting a check |
| `fields` | yes | every field the module can return: name → `type`, `description`, and optionally `"output": true` and `elements` |

Field types:

| Type | JSON value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `string`, `number`, `bool`, `object`, `array` | the JSON type | |
| `bytes` | number of bytes | conditions may use `10MB` etc. |
| `duration` | number of seconds, may be fractional | conditions may use `500ms`, `1h` etc. |

`onecheck validate` checks `params` against `params_schema` only, without
starting a check, so put every rule about params into the schema, including
params that do not go together. A param forbidden in a combination is
written as `false`, which onecheck reports as "not allowed together with the
other params":

```json
"if": { "required": ["path"] },
"then": { "properties": { "exclude_mount": false } }
```

An `array` field whose elements are objects may give the types of the keys
of an element in `elements`:

```json
"disks": {
  "type": "array",
  "description": "one object per disk: name, free, age",
  "elements": { "free": "bytes", "age": "duration" }
}
```

Conditions on those keys then accept unit literals, as on fields of these
types: `disks: { every: { path: free, gt: 5GB } }`. List only the keys that
need it; nested objects and arrays inside an element cannot be typed. A
version of onecheck that does not know `elements` ignores it.

A field with `"output": true` is diagnostic output, like a command's stdout
or a response body. onecheck asks for such fields on every check (they are
added to `fields` of the request) and saves their tail in the result even if
no condition uses them, see
[Output and results](/output-and-results#saved-output). Mark only what
helps to understand a failure and is not expensive to collect.

Declaring fields lets `onecheck validate` reject a condition on a field that
does not exist. Use `"additionalProperties": false` in `params_schema` so
that typos in `params` are caught.

### `onecheck-<name> check`

Reads one request from stdin, prints one response on stdout.

Request:

```json
{
  "protocol": 1,
  "rule": "cache-alive",
  "params": { "addr": "127.0.0.1:6379" },
  "fields": ["ping", "used_memory"],
  "max_field_size": 10485760,
  "timeout_ms": 30000
}
```

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `protocol` | protocol version onecheck is using for this call |
| `rule` | rule name, for the module's own log messages |
| `params` | the rule's `params`, already validated against `params_schema` |
| `fields` | the fields the rule's conditions use, plus the module's output fields unless the rule has `output_tail: 0`. A module may skip collecting everything else, which matters for expensive fields. Empty when the rule has no conditions: then collect only what is cheap |
| `max_field_size` | largest size in bytes of one string value; do not read more than `max_field_size + 1` bytes of anything |
| `timeout_ms` | the rule's timeout; finish before it |

Response:

```json
{
  "fields": { "ping": "PONG", "used_memory": 1048576 },
  "truncated": [],
  "error": null
}
```

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `fields` | field name → value. Omit a field that has no value in this situation |
| `truncated` | names of string fields that were cut to `max_field_size`. onecheck refuses to evaluate conditions on them |
| `error` | `null`, or `{"message": "..."}` when the data could not be collected. `fields` may still carry output fields collected before the failure (what a command printed before its timeout); onecheck saves them and evaluates nothing |

## Rules of behaviour

**Errors versus values.** Return `error` when you could not find out:
connection refused, permission denied, timeout. Return a value when you found
out, even if the answer is bad: an HTTP 500 is `status: 500`, a missing file
is `exists: false`, a non-zero exit code is `exit_code: 3`. An `error` makes
the rule's status `error`; values are judged by the user's conditions.

**Exit code.** Exit with `0` whenever you produced a response, including one
with `error` set. A non-zero exit code, invalid JSON on stdout, or no output
means the module itself is broken; the rule gets status `error`.

**stdout is for the response only.** Write diagnostics to stderr. onecheck
puts a module's stderr into its log at level `debug`.

**Timeouts.** onecheck starts a module in its own process group and kills
the whole group a short moment after `timeout_ms`, and also when onecheck
itself is interrupted. Leave child processes in that group (do not call
`setsid`/`setpgid` for them), so they are cleaned up with the module. Prefer to stop on your own before that and
return an `error` saying what timed out.

**Size limits.** Never read an unbounded amount into memory. Read at most
`max_field_size + 1` bytes; if there was more, cut the value to
`max_field_size` and list the field in `truncated`.

**No state, no side effects.** A module is started fresh for every check and
may run in parallel with other checks, including other instances of itself.

**Environment.** A module inherits onecheck's environment and runs with its
privileges.

## Writing a module in Go

The SDK implements the protocol; you provide a description and one function.

```go
// Command onecheck-uptime reports how long the machine has been up.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strconv"
	"strings"

	"github.com/alekzonder/onecheck/pkg/module"
)

type params struct {
	// File lets tests point the module at a fixture.
	File string `json:"file"`
}

func collect(_ context.Context, req module.Request) (map[string]any, error) {
	p := params{File: "/proc/uptime"}
	if err := module.DecodeParams(req.Params, &p); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	data, err := os.ReadFile(p.File)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err // could not find out: an error
	}
	seconds, err := strconv.ParseFloat(strings.Fields(string(data))[0], 64)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected content of %s", p.File)
	}
	return map[string]any{"uptime": seconds}, nil
}

func main() {
	module.Main(module.Module{
		Description: module.Description{
			Name:        "uptime",
			Version:     "0.1.0",
			Description: "Time since the machine booted",
			ParamsSchema: json.RawMessage(`{
				"type": "object",
				"additionalProperties": false,
				"properties": {"file": {"type": "string"}}
			}`),
			Fields: map[string]module.FieldInfo{
				"uptime": {Type: module.TypeDuration, Description: "time since boot"},
			},
		},
		Collect: collect,
	})
}
```

```sh
go build -o /usr/lib/onecheck/modules/onecheck-uptime .
```

```yaml
rules:
  - name: no-recent-reboot
    module: uptime
    check:
      uptime: { gt: 10m }
```

What the SDK does for you:

- `module.Main` handles `describe` and `check`, fills in `protocol`, applies
  `timeout_ms` to the context passed to `Collect`, turns a returned error
  into the `error` response, and cuts over-long string values while recording
  them in `truncated`.
- `module.DecodeParams` decodes `params` strictly (unknown keys are errors).
- `req.Wants("field")` tells whether a rule uses a field;
  `req.WantsOr("field", cheap)` additionally answers `cheap` when the rule
  has no conditions at all. Use them to skip expensive work.

## Writing a module in another language

Anything that can read stdin and print JSON works. A complete module in
shell:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# onecheck-loadavg: 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages
case "$1" in
  describe)
    cat <<'JSON'
{"protocol": 1, "name": "loadavg", "version": "0.1.0",
 "description": "System load averages",
 "params_schema": {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false},
 "fields": {
   "load1":  {"type": "number", "description": "1 minute load average"},
   "load5":  {"type": "number", "description": "5 minute load average"},
   "load15": {"type": "number", "description": "15 minute load average"}}}
JSON
    ;;
  check)
    cat >/dev/null                      # the request is not needed here
    if read -r l1 l5 l15 _ < /proc/loadavg; then
      printf '{"fields": {"load1": %s, "load5": %s, "load15": %s}, "truncated": [], "error": null}\n' "$l1" "$l5" "$l15"
    else
      printf '{"fields": {}, "truncated": [], "error": {"message": "cannot read /proc/loadavg"}}\n'
    fi
    ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: $0 describe|check" >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
esac
```

## Trying a module by hand

```sh
onecheck-uptime describe | jq .

echo '{"protocol":1,"rule":"t","params":{},"fields":["uptime"],"max_field_size":1048576,"timeout_ms":5000}' \
  | onecheck-uptime check | jq .

onecheck module list          # is it found, is it compatible
onecheck validate             # do my rules fit its params and fields
onecheck --rule no-recent-reboot --log-level debug
```

## Distributing a module

Publish a GitHub release with assets named `onecheck-<name>_<os>_<arch>` and
a `checksums.txt`; then anyone can `onecheck module install <owner/repo>`.
Details: [Module management](/module-management#repositories-of-third-party-modules).

## Protocol versions

The protocol version is a single integer. It changes only when the JSON
exchanged above changes incompatibly. onecheck supports a range of versions
(`onecheck version` prints it) and passes the module's own version back in
each request. Adding optional keys to requests or responses does not change
the version: modules must ignore request keys they do not know, and onecheck
ignores response keys it does not know.

---

# command module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/command

Runs a command and returns its exit code and output.

## Params

Exactly one of `run` and `argv` is required.

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `run` | a command line, executed with `sh -c`; pipes, redirects and variables work |
| `argv` | a list: program and its arguments, executed directly, without a shell |
| `env` | extra environment variables, a mapping of name to value |
| `cwd` | working directory |
| `stdin` | text passed to the command on standard input |

The command inherits onecheck's environment plus `env`. It is killed,
together with everything it started, when the rule's `timeout` expires.

Prefer `argv` when arguments come from elsewhere: nothing is interpreted by a
shell. In `run`, shell variables such as `$HOME`, `$1`, `$$` and `$(...)`
reach the shell untouched; only the `${VAR}` form is expanded by onecheck
from its own environment first (write `$${VAR}` to pass it to the shell
literally).

## Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `exit_code` | number | exit code of the command; `-1` if it was killed by a signal |
| `stdout` | string | standard output |
| `stderr` | string | standard error |
| `duration` | **duration** | how long the command ran |

A non-zero exit code is a value, not an error: check it with `exit_code`. The
rule ends with status `error` when the command could not be run at all
(program not found, not executable, bad `cwd`) or hit the timeout.

Note that a rule does **not** require exit code `0` unless you say so. Add
`exit_code: 0` to `check`.

The tail of `stdout` and `stderr` (the last `10k` of each by default) is saved
in the rule's result on every run, also when no condition mentions them and
when the command hit the timeout, so a failure can be investigated afterwards.
Change the size with `output_tail`, see
[Output and results](/output-and-results#saved-output).

`stdout` and `stderr` are each limited by `run.max_field_size` (default
`10MB`).

Output usually ends with a newline. With `equals` include it (`"active\n"`);
with `matches` use `(?m)` so `$` matches before it: `'(?m)^active$'`.

## Examples

```yaml
rules:
  # exit code only
  - name: nginx-config-valid
    module: command
    params: { argv: [nginx, -t] }
    check:
      exit_code: 0

  # exit code and output
  - name: nginx-active
    module: command
    params: { argv: [systemctl, is-active, nginx] }
    check:
      exit_code: 0
      stdout: { matches: '(?m)^active$' }

  # a shell pipeline producing a number
  - name: not-too-many-processes
    module: command
    params: { run: "ps -e --no-headers | wc -l" }
    check:
      exit_code: 0
      stdout: { matches: '^\s*\d{1,3}\s*$' }      # fewer than 1000

  # JSON output
  - name: queue-short
    module: command
    timeout: 5s
    params: { run: "rabbitmqctl list_queues --formatter json" }
    check:
      exit_code: 0
      stdout:
        json:
          assert:
            - { path: '#(messages>1000)#', length: 0 }

  # nothing alarming on stderr, some output on stdout
  - name: backup-dry-run
    module: command
    params:
      run: "./backup.sh --dry-run"
      cwd: /opt/backup
      env: { BACKUP_TARGET: s3://bucket/prefix }
    check:
      exit_code: { in: [0, 2] }
      stdout: { length: { gt: 0 } }
      stderr: { not_matches: '(?i)error|denied' }
```

---

# cpu module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/cpu

Reports how busy the host's CPUs are, the load average and the number of
cores, so a host that is overloaded for a long time is noticed before its
services slow down. Works on Linux and macOS.

## Params

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `window` | no | how long CPU usage is measured: `500ms`, `5s`, `1m`, or a bare number of seconds; default `1s`; from `100ms` to `5m` |

CPU usage is the difference of two readings of the CPU counters: the module
reads them, waits `window`, and reads them again. Write the window quoted or
not: `window: 5s`, `window: 5`.

The window must be shorter than the rule's `timeout` (default 30s);
otherwise the rule is an `error` at once, without waiting, telling you to
shorten the window or raise `timeout`. A longer window smooths short bursts;
for sustained load combine a short window with `fail_after` (see
[State and events](/state-and-events#thresholds-fail_after-pass_after)).

The module waits only when a `*_percent` field is checked. A rule that
checks only load average answers immediately.

## Fields

Usage over the window, in percent of all cores together (a 4-core host with
one core fully busy shows 25), two decimals:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `usage_percent` | number | busy time: everything except idle and iowait (steal counts as busy) |
| `user_percent` | number | programs (user and nice time) |
| `system_percent` | number | kernel (system, irq and softirq time) |
| `iowait_percent` | number | idle while waiting for disk; **Linux only** |
| `steal_percent` | number | time a virtual machine waited for the hypervisor; **Linux only** |

Without waiting:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `cores` | number | logical CPUs |
| `load1`, `load5`, `load15` | number | load average over 1, 5 and 15 minutes |
| `load1_per_core`, `load5_per_core`, `load15_per_core` | number | load average divided by `cores` |

### Which field to use

- **CPU busy:** `usage_percent`. It includes steal time, so on a virtual
  machine a high `usage_percent` with a high `steal_percent` means the
  hypervisor is short of CPU, not your programs; check
  `user_percent`/`system_percent` for what your programs use.
- **Load:** prefer `*_per_core` to `load*`: the same threshold then fits
  hosts with any number of cores. Load above 1 per core means work is
  waiting for a CPU. `load5`/`load15` react slower and ignore short spikes.
- On Linux load average also counts processes waiting for disk, so high
  load with low `usage_percent` and high `iowait_percent` points to slow
  storage rather than to the CPU.

Which fields are present:

- `iowait_percent` and `steal_percent` are missing on macOS, which does not
  report these times; a condition on them fails with "got nothing (path is
  missing)".
- `*_percent` fields are missing when no rule condition asks for them.
  On macOS a rule that checks only `iowait_percent`/`steal_percent` does
  not wait the window.

Inside a container the module reports the host's CPUs and load, not the
container's limits.

Reading the counters failing is an `error`, not a `fail`.

## Examples

```yaml
# conf.d/cpu.yaml
rules:
  # busy for three runs in a row (three minutes from cron)
  - name: cpu
    module: cpu
    params: { window: 5s }
    fail_after: 3
    check:
      usage_percent: { lt: 90 }

  # load too high for the number of cores; answers without waiting
  - name: load
    module: cpu
    check:
      load5_per_core: { lt: 1.5 }
```

A failure names the rule and the value:

```
FAIL   cpu   (cpu, 5006ms)
       usage_percent: expected lt 90, got 97.32
```

---

# disk module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/disk

Reports free space and inodes of one filesystem, or of every filesystem of
the host, so a disk that is filling up
is noticed before services on it start to fail. Running out of inodes (many
small files: sessions, caches, mail queues) breaks writes just like running
out of space, so check both.

## Params

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `path` | no | a mount point, any path inside a filesystem, or a device; without it [all filesystems](#all-filesystems) are listed |
| `exclude_fstype` | no | without `path`: list of shell patterns of filesystem types to leave out |
| `exclude_mount` | no | without `path`: list of shell patterns of mount points to leave out |

- A mount point (`/var`) or any path inside a filesystem
  (`/var/lib/postgresql`): the filesystem holding that path is reported.
  Symlinks are followed.
- A device under `/dev/` (`/dev/sda1`, `/dev/mapper/vg-data`,
  `/dev/disk/by-uuid/...`): its mount point is looked up in the mount table.
  Symlinks are resolved on both sides, so any name of the device works.
  A root filesystem listed in the mount table under a name that does not
  exist on disk (`/dev/root` on some systems) cannot be found by device;
  use its mount point, `/`, instead.

A rule with `path` checks one filesystem. A rule without it checks all of
them at once, including disks added later.

## Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `total` | **bytes** | size of the filesystem |
| `free` | **bytes** | space available to ordinary users, like `df` "Avail" |
| `used` | **bytes** | used space: `total` minus all free blocks |
| `used_percent` | number | `used / (used + free) * 100`, like `df` "Use%" |
| `inodes_total` | number | inodes of the filesystem |
| `inodes_free` | number | free inodes |
| `inodes_used` | number | used inodes |
| `inodes_used_percent` | number | `inodes_used / inodes_total * 100` |
| `mountpoint` | string | where the filesystem is mounted |
| `device` | string | the mounted device, as in the mount table |
| `fstype` | string | filesystem type, e.g. `ext4`, `xfs`, `apfs` |

Percentages have two decimals (`89.1`); `df` rounds them up (`90%`).

Blocks reserved for root (5 % on ext4 by default) count as unavailable, as in
`df`: `used_percent` reaches 100 when ordinary users can no longer write,
even though root still can.

**bytes** fields accept unit literals in conditions: `free: { gt: 5GB }`.
See [Checks](/checks#gt-gte-lt-lte).

Which fields are present:

- `inodes_*` are missing on filesystems without a fixed number of inodes
  (btrfs and some others report 0). A condition on them then fails with
  "got nothing (path is missing)"; leave inode conditions out for such disks.
  ZFS reports an inode count that grows and shrinks with free space, so
  `inodes_used_percent` on ZFS mostly repeats `used_percent`.
- `mountpoint`, `device` and `fstype` are missing if the mount table cannot
  be read; the numbers are still reported.

A path that does not exist, a device that is not mounted, or a filesystem
that cannot be queried is an `error`, not a `fail`.

A rule without `check` passes whenever the numbers could be read, as with any
module, so always give thresholds.

## All filesystems

Without `path` the module returns the filesystems of the host, and nothing
else:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `filesystems` | array | the filesystems, sorted by mount point |
| `count` | number | how many there are |

Each element has the fields of a single filesystem described above:
`mountpoint`, `device`, `fstype`, `total`, `free`, `used` (**bytes**),
`used_percent`, and the `inodes_*` fields where the filesystem has a fixed
number of inodes. Conditions go through
[`every` / `some` and `path`](/checks#every-some); `total`, `free` and
`used` accept unit literals there too.

```yaml
- name: disks
  module: disk
  check:
    count: { gte: 1 }
    filesystems:
      every:
        - { path: used_percent, lt: 90 }
        - { path: free, gt: 5GB }
```

A failure names the filesystem:

```
FAIL   disks   (disk, 5ms)
       filesystems.0.used_percent: expected lt 90, got 93.74 (element {"device":"/dev/vda1","free":10046664704,"fstype":"ext4","inodes_free":8166363,"inodes_total":10383360,"inodes_used":2216997,"inodes_used_percent":21.35,"mountpoint":"/","total":168998809600,"used":150345506816,"used_percent":93.74})
```

**Which filesystems are listed.** Only those that hold data and can fill up:

- the device is a path (`/dev/sda1`, `/dev/mapper/vg-data`), or the type is
  a network or pooled one: `zfs`, `nfs`, `nfs4`, `cifs`, `smb3`, `smbfs`,
  `ceph`, `9p`, `virtiofs`, `lustre`, `fuse.glusterfs`, `fuse.sshfs`;
- not a read-only image or a container layer: `squashfs` (snap), `iso9660`,
  `udf`, `erofs`, `cramfs`, `overlay`;
- not of size zero.

So `proc`, `sysfs`, `tmpfs`, cgroups, the overlays of containers and snap
images are never in the list.

**One device once.** A device mounted in several places (bind mounts, Docker
volumes, btrfs subvolumes) is listed once, at its shortest mount point. ZFS
datasets are separate devices and are all listed.

**Narrowing the list.** `exclude_fstype` and `exclude_mount` take
[`glob` patterns](/checks#glob-not_glob):

```yaml
- name: disks
  module: disk
  params:
    exclude_fstype: [nfs*, vfat]
    exclude_mount: [/mnt/backup, "/media/*"]
  check:
    filesystems: { every: { path: used_percent, lt: 90 } }
```

A filesystem that needs its own limits gets a rule with `path` and is
