excluded here. `exclude_mount` matches the mount point the filesystem is
listed at.

Inodes: a filesystem without a fixed number of inodes has no `inodes_*`
keys, and `every` would fail on it with "path is missing". Check inodes
only where they exist:

```yaml
    filesystems.#(inodes_total>0)#:
      every: { path: inodes_used_percent, lt: 90 }
```

Things to know:

- If a listed filesystem cannot be queried (a stale NFS mount, no
  permission), the rule is an `error` that names the mount point: fix the
  mount or put it into `exclude_mount`. A network mount that hangs does not
  answer at all: the rule then ends with a timeout `error` that names no
  mount point. An excluded filesystem is not touched, so such a mount can be
  left out.
- No filesystems after the exclusions is `filesystems: []`, `count: 0`, not
  an error; `count: { gte: 1 }` catches a list that became empty.
- The fields of a single filesystem (`used_percent`, ...) are missing at the
  top level in this mode, and `filesystems`, `count` are missing with
  `path`. `exclude_fstype` and `exclude_mount` together with `path` are an
  error.
- macOS: the APFS volumes of one container are separate devices sharing the
  same space and are all listed; `exclude_mount: ["/System/Volumes/*"]`
  leaves the system ones out.

## Examples

```yaml
# conf.d/disks.yaml
rules:
  # recommended thresholds for a system disk
  - name: disk-root
    module: disk
    params: { path: / }
    check:
      used_percent: { lt: 90 }
      inodes_used_percent: { lt: 90 }

  # data disk: alert by absolute free space, after two runs in a row
  - name: disk-data
    module: disk
    fail_after: 2
    params: { path: /var/lib/postgresql }
    check:
      free: { gt: 20GB }
      used_percent: { lt: 85 }

  # by device name; also make sure it is mounted where expected
  - name: disk-backup
    module: disk
    params: { path: /dev/mapper/vg-backup }
    check:
      mountpoint: /backup
      used_percent: { lt: 95 }
```

A failure names the rule and the value:

```
FAIL   disk-root   (disk, 1ms)
       used_percent: expected lt 90, got 93.4
```

---

# docker module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/docker

Reports Docker containers, so you know that the containers which must serve
are running and healthy, that nothing restarts in a loop or dies of running
out of memory, and that no unknown container is running on the host.
Works on Linux and macOS with Docker, Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima,
rootless Docker and Podman (its Docker-compatible API).

The module always returns the same fields: the list of containers that
match the params, and their number. Params only narrow the list.

## Params

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | no | container name, exact (`nginx`) or a shell pattern (`app-*`), without the leading `/` |
| `label` | no | `key` (the label is set) or `key=value`, e.g. `com.docker.compose.project=shop` |
| `host` | no | where Docker is: `unix:///path/to/docker.sock` or `tcp://host:port`; found automatically when omitted |

Without `name` and `label` every container is listed, running or not (like
`docker ps -a`). With both, a container must match both. A filter that
matches nothing gives `count: 0`, not an error.

Patterns use the [`glob` syntax](/checks#glob-not_glob): `*`, `?`,
`[abc]`, `[!abc]`.

### Where Docker is

When `host` is not set, the module takes the first of:

1. the `DOCKER_HOST` environment variable;
2. the current Docker context (`DOCKER_CONTEXT`, else `docker context use`
   saved in `~/.docker/config.json`; `DOCKER_CONFIG` moves `~/.docker`). The
   `default` context means "no context";
3. the first socket that exists:
   - `/var/run/docker.sock`
   - `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock` (rootless Docker)
   - macOS: `~/.docker/run/docker.sock` (Docker Desktop),
     `~/.orbstack/run/docker.sock`, `~/.colima/default/docker.sock`
   - `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock`, `/run/podman/podman.sock`

When onecheck runs from cron or a systemd timer, its environment usually has
no `DOCKER_HOST` and maybe no `HOME`: set `host` in the rule if Docker is not
at one of the default sockets.

Only `unix://` and `tcp://` (plain HTTP) addresses are supported. A `tcp://`
address without a port uses 2375. TLS (`DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY`, a context with
TLS certificates) and `ssh://` are not supported and give an error.

Every error names the address and where it came from:

```
docker at unix:///var/run/docker.sock (default socket): dial unix /var/run/docker.sock: connect: permission denied; add the user onecheck runs as to the docker group or run it as root
```

Reading the Docker socket is equivalent to root access on the host; give
onecheck that access knowingly.

## Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `containers` | array | matching containers sorted by name |
| `count` | number | number of matching containers |

Each element of `containers` has all of these keys:

| Key | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | container name, without the leading `/` |
| `id` | string | short id (12 characters) |
| `image` | string | image the container was created from, as written in `docker run` or compose: `nginx:1.27`, `registry.local/app:3` |
| `state` | string | `created`, `running`, `paused`, `restarting`, `removing`, `exited`, `dead` |
| `health` | string | `healthy`, `unhealthy`, `starting`; `none` when the container has no healthcheck |
| `restart_count` | number | restarts done by the restart policy (`restart: always`, ...) |
| `exit_code` | number | exit code of the last run; 0 while it runs |
| `oom_killed` | bool | the last run was killed for running out of memory |
| `uptime_seconds` | **duration** | seconds since the container started, while it is `running` or `restarting`; otherwise 0 |
| `labels` | object | container labels |

Element keys are checked with paths (`containers.0.state`) or with
[`every` / `some` and `path`](/checks#every-some). `uptime_seconds` is a
**duration**: `{ path: uptime_seconds, gt: 1h }` works, as does a plain
number of seconds.

A rule that only checks `count` makes one request to Docker. A rule that
checks `containers` asks Docker about each matching container too.

## Recipes

### A container must run

```yaml
- name: nginx
  module: docker
  params: { name: nginx }
  check:
    count: 1                                    # it exists
    containers.0.state: running
    containers.0.health: { not_equals: unhealthy }
```

`count: 1` first: without it a missing container would only show as a
missing path.

### No unknown containers

Every running container must be allowed by its name, a name pattern or an
image pattern. Allowing does not require: a container that is not running is
not reported here (check required ones with the rule above).

```yaml
- name: no-unknown-containers
  module: docker
  check:
    containers.#(state=="running")#:
      every:
        any:
          - { path: name,  in: [nginx, postgres] }
          - { path: name,  glob: "app-*" }
          - { path: image, glob: "registry.local/*" }
```

Drop `#(state=="running")#` to require that stopped containers are known as
well.

### A whole compose project

```yaml
- name: shop
  module: docker
  params: { label: com.docker.compose.project=shop }
  check:
    count: { gte: 3 }
    containers:
      every:
        - { path: state, equals: running }
        - { path: health, not_equals: unhealthy }
```

### Crash loops and OOM kills

```yaml
- name: containers-stable
  module: docker
  check:
    containers:
      every:
        - { path: restart_count, lt: 5 }
        - { path: oom_killed, equals: false }
```

`restart_count` grows for the life of the container and is reset when it is
recreated (a new deploy), so pick a limit above what a normal deploy cycle
reaches.

### Image of a container

```yaml
- name: api-version
  module: docker
  params: { name: api }
  check:
    containers.0.image: { glob: "registry.local/api:2.*" }
```

## Output

```
FAIL   no-unknown-containers  (docker, 140ms)  [transition: fail]
       containers.#(state=="running")#.2: expected any [{"in":["nginx","postgres"],"path":"name"},{"glob":"app-*","path":"name"},{"glob":"registry.local/*","path":"image"}], got {"exit_code":0,"health":"none","id":"9c1e2b7d4a10","image":"xmrig/xmrig","name":"miner","oom_killed":false,"restart_count":0,"state":"running","uptime_seconds":312}
FAIL   shop                   (docker, 110ms)  [transition: fail]
       containers.1.state: expected equals "running", got "exited" (element {"exit_code":137,"health":"none","id":"3f2a90c1d5e7","image":"registry.local/shop-worker:4","name":"shop-worker-1","oom_killed":true,"restart_count":0,"state":"exited","uptime_seconds":0})
```

The index (`.2`, `.1`) is the position in the (filtered) list; the
element's keys in the message (all but `labels`) tell which container it is.

---

# file module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/file

Inspects one path: a file, a directory or a symlink.

## Params

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `path` | yes | the path to inspect |

Glob patterns are not supported: one rule looks at one path.

## Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `exists` | bool | whether the path exists |
| `type` | string | `file`, `dir`, `symlink` or `other` (socket, device, ...) |
| `size` | **bytes** | file size; for a directory the total size of all files below it |
| `age` | **duration** | time since the last modification |
| `mode` | string | permission bits as four octal digits, e.g. `"0640"` |
| `owner` | string | owner user name (the numeric id if it has no name) |
| `group` | string | owner group name (the numeric id if it has no name) |
| `content` | string | content of a regular file |
| `count` | number | number of entries directly in a directory |
| `target` | string | where a symlink points, exactly as stored in the link |

**bytes** and **duration** fields accept unit literals in conditions:
`size: { lt: 10MB }`, `age: { lt: 1h }`. See [Checks](/checks#gt-gte-lt-lte).

Which fields are present:

| The path is | Fields returned |
|---|---|
| missing | `exists: false` only |
| a regular file | everything except `count` and `target` |
| a directory | everything except `content` and `target` |
| a symlink to something that exists | `type: symlink`, `target`, and all other fields describing **what the link points to** |
| a dangling symlink | `exists: false`, `type: symlink`, `target` |

A condition on a field that is not returned fails with "path is missing", so
`size: { gt: 0 }` on a missing file fails as it should.

Only the fields a rule uses are collected. In particular `content` is read,
and a directory's total `size` is computed, only when `check` mentions them.

`content` is limited by `run.max_field_size` (default `10MB`). A condition on
a larger file ends the rule with status `error`; check `size` or raise the
limit.

A path that cannot be inspected at all (permission denied on a parent
directory, unreadable file when `content` is requested) is an `error`, not a
`fail`.

## Examples

```yaml
rules:
  # exists, right owner and permissions
  - name: sshd-config
    module: file
    params: { path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config }
    check:
      exists: true
      type: file
      owner: root
      mode: "0600"

  # must not exist
  - name: no-maintenance-flag
    module: file
    params: { path: /var/www/maintenance.flag }
    check:
      exists: false

  # a backup was written during the last day and is not suspiciously small
  - name: backup-fresh
    module: file
    params: { path: /backup/latest.tar.gz }
    check:
      exists: true
      age: { lt: 25h }
      size: { gt: 100MB }

  # content: substring, regular expression
  - name: nginx-listens-443
    module: file
    params: { path: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf }
    check:
      content:
        contains: "listen 443"
        not_matches: '(?m)^\s*server_tokens\s+on'

  # content as JSON
  - name: app-config
    module: file
    params: { path: /etc/app/config.json }
    check:
      content:
        json:
          assert:
            - { path: db.host, equals: localhost }
            - { path: features, type: array }

  # directory: total size and number of entries
  - name: spool-not-growing
    module: file
    params: { path: /var/spool/app }
    check:
      type: dir
      size: { lt: 1GB }
      count: { lt: 500 }

  # a symlink points where it should
  - name: current-release
    module: file
    params: { path: /srv/app/current }
    check:
      exists: true                       # the target exists
      type: symlink
      target: { starts_with: /srv/app/releases/ }
```

---

# http module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/http

Makes one HTTP or HTTPS request.

## Params

| Key | Required | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | yes | | `http://` or `https://` URL |
| `method` | no | `GET` | HTTP method |
| `headers` | no | | request headers, a mapping of name to value |
| `body` | no | | request body |
| `follow_redirects` | no | `true` | follow redirects; with `false` the redirect response itself is returned |
| `insecure_skip_verify` | no | `false` | do not verify the server's TLS certificate |

The request is limited by the rule's `timeout`. Proxy settings are taken from
the usual `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` / `NO_PROXY` environment variables.

Secrets can be passed through the environment, see
[Configuration](/configuration#environment-variables-in-params):

```yaml
headers:
  Authorization: "Bearer ${API_TOKEN}"
```

When a request fails, the error names the URL without its query string and
without a user name and password, including the URL of a redirect:
`Get "https://example.com/health": connection refused`. A token passed as
`?token=...` does not end up in results, events, logs or notifications.

## Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `status` | number | HTTP status code |
| `headers` | object | response headers; names in **lower case**, repeated headers joined with `, ` |
| `body` | string | response body |
| `duration` | **duration** | time from sending the request until the whole body was read |
| `tls_expires_in` | **duration** | time until the server certificate expires; https only |

**duration** fields accept unit literals: `duration: { lt: 500ms }`,
`tls_expires_in: { gt: 14d }`.

Address a single header as `headers.<name>`, always in lower case:
`headers.content-type`.

A response with any status code is a successful collection: `404` and `500`
are values of `status` to be checked. The rule ends with status `error`, not
`fail`, when no response could be obtained: DNS failure, connection refused,
TLS handshake or certificate error, timeout.

`body` is limited by `run.max_field_size` (default `10MB`); a condition on a
larger body ends the rule with status `error`.

The tail of `body` (the last `10k` by default) and the `headers` are saved in
the rule's result on every run, also when no condition mentions them, so a
failed `status: 200` can be investigated afterwards. Change the size with
`output_tail`, or set `output_tail: 0` for responses that hold secrets, see
[Output and results](/output-and-results#saved-output).

`tls_expires_in` is absent for plain `http://` URLs, so a condition on it
fails there.

## Examples

```yaml
rules:
  # status and substring
  - name: site-up
    module: http
    timeout: 10s
    params: { url: https://example.com/ }
    check:
      status: 200
      body: { contains: "Welcome" }

  # several acceptable statuses, headers, response time
  - name: api-root
    module: http
    params: { url: https://api.example.com/ }
    check:
      status: { in: [200, 204] }
      headers.content-type: { starts_with: application/json }
      headers.strict-transport-security: { exists: true }
      headers.x-powered-by: { exists: false }
      duration: { lt: 1s }

  # JSON body: values, presence of keys, array contents
  - name: api-health
    module: http
    params:
      url: https://api.example.com/health
      headers: { Authorization: "Bearer ${API_TOKEN}" }
    check:
      status: 200
      body:
        json:
          assert:
            - { path: status, equals: ok }
            - { path: version, exists: true }
            - { path: checks.#, gte: 1 }
            - { path: 'checks.#(state!="ok")#', length: 0 }

  # JSON body validated with a JSON Schema
  - name: api-contract
    module: http
    params: { url: https://api.example.com/v1/users/1 }
    check:
      body:
        json:
          schema:
            type: object
            required: [id, email, roles]
            properties:
              id: { type: integer }
              email: { type: string, pattern: "@" }
              roles: { type: array, items: { type: string } }

  # POST with a body
  - name: login-works
    module: http
    params:
      url: https://example.com/api/login
      method: POST
      headers: { Content-Type: application/json }
      body: '{"user":"probe","password":"${PROBE_PASSWORD}"}'
    check:
      status: 200
      body: { json: { assert: [ { path: token, type: string } ] } }

  # a redirect is in place
  - name: http-redirects-to-https
    module: http
    params:
      url: http://example.com/
      follow_redirects: false
    check:
      status: { in: [301, 308] }
      headers.location: { starts_with: "https://" }

  # certificate lifetime
  - name: certificate
    module: http
    params: { url: https://example.com/ }
    check:
      tls_expires_in: { gt: 14d }
```

---

# memory module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/memory

Reports physical memory and swap usage of the host, so memory running out
is noticed before the system starts swapping heavily or killing processes.
Works on Linux and macOS.

## Params

None. `params` may be omitted.

## Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `total` | **bytes** | physical memory |
| `available` | **bytes** | memory that can be given to programs without swapping |
| `used` | **bytes** | `total` minus `available` |
| `used_percent` | number | `used / total * 100` |
| `swap_total` | **bytes** | swap size |
| `swap_used` | **bytes** | swap in use |
| `swap_free` | **bytes** | free swap |
| `swap_used_percent` | number | `swap_used / swap_total * 100`; 0 when there is no swap |

Percentages have two decimals.

On Linux `available` is the kernel's `MemAvailable`: page cache and other
memory the kernel can reclaim at once are not counted in `used`, as in the
"available" column of `free`. A host with a large file cache therefore
shows low `used_percent` even though little memory is "free"; that is
normal.

On macOS `available` is free plus inactive memory. `used` then still
includes active file cache and compressed and wired memory, so it reads
higher than "Memory Used" in Activity Monitor, often 75–90 % on an idle Mac.
On Macs prefer a threshold on `available` (`available: { gt: 2GB }`) or a
higher `used_percent` limit.

macOS has no fixed swap: it adds swap files as needed, so `swap_total`
grows and shrinks, and a high `swap_used_percent` there is less alarming
than on Linux.

**bytes** fields accept unit literals in conditions:
`available: { gt: 1GB }`. See [Checks](/checks#gt-gte-lt-lte).

Inside a container the module reports the host's memory, not the
container's limit.

Reading memory or swap failing is an `error`, not a `fail`.

## Examples

```yaml
# conf.d/memory.yaml
rules:
  - name: memory
    module: memory
    check:
      used_percent: { lt: 90 }
      swap_used_percent: { lt: 50 }

  # a small host: keep at least 512 MB available
  - name: memory-available
    module: memory
    check:
      available: { gt: 512MB }
```

A failure names the rule and the value:

```
FAIL   memory   (memory, 2ms)
       used_percent: expected lt 90, got 93.41
```

---

# ports module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/ports

Reports the TCP and UDP ports the host listens on, so you know that nothing
unexpected is exposed and that every port which must serve is open.
Linux only: the data comes from the kernel (`/proc/net`), the same that
`ss -tuln` shows. No root is needed and no external command is run.

A port cannot be reached from outside when nothing listens on an outside
address, whatever the firewall says. Ports published by Docker are
listening sockets too (of `docker-proxy`), so they are in the list even
though Docker opens them past `ufw`.

The module always returns the same fields: the list of listening sockets
that match the params, and their number. Params only narrow the list.

## Params

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `proto` | no | `tcp` or `udp`; both when omitted |
| `interface` | no | only sockets bound to an address of this interface, e.g. `eth0`, or to all addresses |

Without `interface` the list has every socket except those bound to a
loopback address (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`): what other machines could reach.

With `interface` the list has the sockets bound to an address of that
interface and the sockets bound to all addresses (`0.0.0.0`, `::`), which
answer on every interface. `interface: lo` lists what listens locally: the
whole `127.0.0.0/8` network and `::1`. An interface that does not exist is
an error.

`interface` selects by the address a socket is bound to. It is not a
guarantee about packets: Linux answers on one interface for an address of
another unless the firewall or `rp_filter` forbids it. Sockets bound to a
broadcast or multicast address, or to an address no interface has, are
listed only without `interface`.

## Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `listening` | array | listening sockets sorted by proto, port, address |
| `count` | number | number of listening sockets |

Each element of `listening` has all of these keys:

| Key | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `proto` | string | `tcp`, `udp` |
| `port` | number | port number |
| `address` | string | `0.0.0.0` or `::` for all addresses, otherwise the address the socket is bound to |
| `family` | string | `ipv4`, `ipv6` |
| `interface` | string | interface that has the address; `any` for all addresses; `""` when no interface has it |
| `process` | string | name of the process that holds the socket; `""` when onecheck may not see it |

TCP sockets are those in the LISTEN state. UDP has no such state: the list
has the UDP sockets without a remote address, the ones `ss -uln` shows.

A service that opens an IPv4 and an IPv6 socket gives two elements
(`0.0.0.0` and `::`). Many programs open only the `::` socket and serve
IPv4 through it: that is one element with `family: ipv6`, so do not use
`family` to tell whether a port answers on IPv4. Several sockets on the same proto, address and port (worker
processes) are one element and count once.

`process` is filled for the processes onecheck may inspect: all of them as
root, only its own user's otherwise. When several processes hold the
socket, the one with the lowest pid is named: for a socket-activated
service (`ssh.socket`, `docker.socket`) that is `systemd`. An address that
two interfaces have is shown with the first interface by name. A rule that only checks `count` does
not look processes up.

## Recipes

### No unknown ports

Every listening socket must be an allowed one. Anything else is a failure
that names the port, the address and the process.

```yaml
- name: no-unknown-ports
  module: ports
  check:
    listening:
      every:
        any:
          - { path: port, in: [22, 80, 443] }
          - { path: port, gte: 60001, lte: 60010 }        # mosh
```

To allow a port only for one protocol or on one interface, put the
conditions of one alternative into `all`:

```yaml
          - all:
              - { path: port, equals: 51820 }
              - { path: proto, equals: udp }
          - all:
              - { path: port, in: [8200, 8201] }
              - { path: interface, equals: wg0 }          # only on the VPN
```

### A port must be open

```yaml
- name: web-ports
  module: ports
  params: { proto: tcp }
  check:
    listening.#.port: { contains: 443 }
```

`listening.#.port` is the list of port numbers. Write one rule per protocol,
or select the protocol in the path:
`listening.#(proto=="udp")#.port: { contains: 51820 }`.

### Both in one rule

```yaml
- name: tcp-ports
  module: ports
  params: { proto: tcp }
  check:
    listening:
      every: { path: port, in: [22, 80, 443] }
    listening.#.port:
      all:
        - { contains: 80 }
        - { contains: 443 }
```

### One interface

```yaml
- name: public-interface
  module: ports
  params: { interface: eth0, proto: tcp }
  check:
    listening:
      every: { path: port, in: [22, 443] }
```

### A local service is up

```yaml
- name: postgres-listens
  module: ports
  params: { interface: lo, proto: tcp }
  check:
    listening.#.port: { contains: 5432 }
```

## Limits

- **The firewall is not consulted.** A port that listens on `0.0.0.0` and
  is hidden only by the firewall is in the list: allow it in the rule or
  bind the service to `127.0.0.1`. A port that listens but is blocked by the
  firewall still counts as open. A firewall of the cloud provider is not
  visible from the host at all.
- **UDP is noisier than TCP.** Programs open unconnected UDP sockets on
  random ports for a short time (DNS clients, DHCP, mosh sessions). When a
  "no unknown ports" rule fails now and then on UDP, check only TCP
  (`proto: tcp`) or allow the port range.
- A socket bound to a device rather than an address (`SO_BINDTODEVICE`) is
  shown with the address it is bound to, usually `0.0.0.0`.
- Port forwarding done only in the firewall (DNAT without a listening
  socket, Docker with `userland-proxy: false`) is not seen.

## Output

```
FAIL   no-unknown-ports  (ports, 20ms)  [transition: fail]
       listening.3: expected any [{"in":[22,80,443],"path":"port"},{"gte":60001,"lte":60010,"path":"port"}], got {"address":"0.0.0.0","family":"ipv4","interface":"any","port":8080,"process":"docker-proxy","proto":"tcp"}
FAIL   web-ports         (ports, 19ms)  [transition: fail]
       listening.#.port: expected contains 443, got [22,22,80]
```

---

# systemd module
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/modules/systemd

Reports the state of one systemd unit, or lists the units in a state such
as `failed`, so you know that services which must
serve are running and start on boot, that units which must stay off are
stopped and will not come back after a reboot, and that scheduled jobs
(timers) really run and succeed, and that nothing on the host is failed
without anybody having listed it.

Works with any unit type: `service`, `timer`, `socket`, `mount`, `path`,
`target`, ... It calls `systemctl show`, so it needs systemd; on other
systems (macOS, Linux without systemd) every check is an `error`.

## Params

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `unit` | one of `unit`, `state` | unit name, e.g. `nginx.service`, `backup.timer`, `docker.socket` |
| `state` | one of `unit`, `state` | instead of a unit: list the units in this state, e.g. `failed`; see [Units in a state](#units-in-a-state) |
| `exclude` | no | with `state`: list of shell patterns of unit names to leave out |
| `user` | no | `true` checks the user's own service manager (`systemctl --user`); default `false` |
| `properties` | no | with `unit`: list of extra `systemctl show` property names, returned in the `properties` field |

A name without a suffix (`nginx`) is understood by systemd as a service.
Name exactly one unit: patterns (`*`, `?`, `[`) are rejected, because
systemd would report several units at once. Escaped names such as
`dev-disk-by\x2dlabel-root.device` work as `systemctl` shows them.

`user: true` is for onecheck running as an ordinary user. The user's service
manager must be running: for cron or a timer outside a login session enable
lingering (`loginctl enable-linger <user>`). If `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` is not set,
the module uses `/run/user/<uid>`. Checking another user's units from root is
not supported.

A rule with `unit` checks one unit; write one rule per unit that must run
or must stay off. A rule with `state` looks at the whole host.

## Fields

All units:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `load_state` | string | `loaded`, `not-found`, `masked`, `bad-setting`, `error` |
| `active_state` | string | `active`, `inactive`, `failed`, `activating`, `deactivating`, `reloading` |
| `sub_state` | string | type-specific state: `running`, `exited`, `dead`, `waiting`, `listening`, ... |
| `unit_file_state` | string | `enabled`, `disabled`, `static`, `masked`, `indirect`, `generated`, ...; empty string if systemd reports none (e.g. the unit does not exist) |
| `result` | string | result of the unit's last run: `success`, `exit-code`, `signal`, `timeout`, `core-dump`, ... |
| `description` | string | unit description |
| `state_age` | **duration** | time since the last change of the active or sub state |

Services:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `restarts` | number | automatic restarts (`Restart=`) since the service was started: a crash loop shows here |
| `main_pid` | number | main process id, 0 if not running |
| `exit_status` | number | exit status of the last main process |

Timers:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `service` | string | the unit the timer starts |
| `last_trigger_age` | **duration** | time since the timer last fired; missing if it has not fired |
| `idle_age` | **duration** | time since the timer last fired or, if systemd does not know when it last fired (e.g. after a reboot without `Persistent=true`), since the timer was activated |
| `next_trigger_in` | **duration** | time until the next calendar (`OnCalendar=`) run; missing if none is scheduled, so always missing for timers with only `OnBootSec=`/`OnActiveSec=`/`OnUnitActiveSec=` |
| `service_result` | string | result of the last run of the started unit: `success`, `exit-code`, ... |
| `service_exit_status` | number | exit status of the started service's last main process |
| `service_active_state` | string | active state of the started unit |

Raw:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `properties` | object | `{Name: value}` for each name in `params.properties`; integers (sizes, counts, ids) as numbers, everything else as text exactly as `systemctl show` prints it (`infinity`, `yes`, `[not set]`); a name systemd does not know is missing |

**duration** fields accept unit literals in conditions:
`idle_age: { lt: 25h }`. See [Checks](/checks#gt-gte-lt-lte).

### Which field to use

- **Must run:** `active_state: active`. **Must be stopped:**
  `active_state: { not_equals: active }` (a `failed` unit is not running
  either). A typo in the unit name makes "must be stopped" pass, because a
  unit that does not exist is not running: add `load_state: loaded` to
  rules for units that must be installed.
- **Starts on boot / must not:** `unit_file_state`. `enabled` starts on boot;
  `disabled` and `masked` do not (`masked` cannot even be started by hand).
  `static` units have no `[Install]` section and are started by something
  else.
- **Timer fires regularly:** prefer `idle_age` to `last_trigger_age`. A timer
  without `Persistent=true` forgets when it last fired on every reboot;
  `last_trigger_age` is then missing and a condition on it fails until the
  timer fires again, up to a whole period after each boot. `idle_age` counts
  from the timer's activation in that case, and still fails when an active
  timer has not fired for longer than the threshold. When systemd knows the
  last run, `idle_age` equals `last_trigger_age`, so restarting a timer that
  stopped firing does not hide it.
- **The job succeeds:** `service_result: success`. Prefer it to
  `service_exit_status`: a unit may declare other exit codes successful
  (`SuccessExitStatus=`), and `service_result` already accounts for that.
  Before the job has run for the first time since boot it is `success`.
- Anything else: name the property in `params.properties` and check
  `properties.<Name>`, e.g. `properties.MemoryCurrent`.

Which fields are present:

- Service fields only for services, timer fields only for timers.
- A unit that does not exist is not an error: systemd reports it with
  `load_state: not-found` and `active_state: inactive` (and default values
  such as `result: success`, `restarts: 0` for services). "Must run" then fails
  with a clear message, "must be stopped" passes.
- Older systemd versions do not have some properties (`NRestarts` appeared in
  systemd 235); their fields are then missing and conditions on them fail
  with "got nothing (path is missing)".

`systemctl` missing or failing (e.g. no user service manager for
`user: true`) is an `error`, not a `fail`; systemd's message is shown.

A rule without `check` passes whenever the state could be read, as with any
module, so always say what you expect.

## Units in a state

With `state` instead of `unit` the module returns the units systemd reports
in that state (`systemctl list-units --all --state=<state>`), and nothing
else:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `units` | array | the units in that state, sorted by name |
| `names` | array | their names, as strings |
| `count` | number | how many there are |

Each element of `units` has `name`, `load_state`, `active_state`,
`sub_state` and `description`.

The check it is made for is "nothing is failed":

```yaml
- name: no-failed-units
  module: systemd
  params: { state: failed }
  check:
    names: []
```

`names: []` passes while the list is empty and otherwise names the units:

```
FAIL   no-failed-units   (systemd, 14ms)
       names: expected equals [], got ["backup@daily.service","nginx.service"]
```

`count: 0` means the same but its message only says how many.

`exclude` leaves units out by name, with the
[`glob` syntax](/checks#glob-not_glob): `*`, `?`, `[abc]`, `[!abc]`.

```yaml
- name: no-failed-units
  module: systemd
  params:
    state: failed
    exclude: ["user@*.service", "motd-news.service"]
  check:
    names: []
```

- Nothing in the state gives `names: []`, `units: []`, `count: 0`, not an
  error.
- `state` is a load or active state of systemd: `failed`, `active`,
  `inactive`, `activating`, `deactivating`, `reloading`, `maintenance`,
  `refreshing`, `loaded`, `not-found`, `bad-setting`, `error`, `masked`.
  Any other name is an error of the rule: systemd itself answers a state it
  does not know with an empty list, and a misspelt `faild` would pass
  forever.
- `user: true` lists the units of the user's service manager.
- The fields of a single unit (`active_state`, `restarts`, ...) are missing
  in this mode, and `units`, `names`, `count` are missing with `unit`.
  `properties` works only with `unit`, `exclude` only with `state`.
- For details of a unit in the list (restarts, timer runs), write a rule
  with `unit`.

## Examples

```yaml
# conf.d/services.yaml
rules:
  # must run and start on boot
  - name: nginx
    module: systemd
    params: { unit: nginx.service }
    check:
      active_state: active
      unit_file_state: enabled

  # must be stopped and not come back after a reboot
  - name: telnet-off
    module: systemd
    params: { unit: telnet.socket }
    check:
      active_state: { not_equals: active }
      unit_file_state: { in: [disabled, masked, ""] }

  # running, and not restarting over and over
  - name: app-stable
    module: systemd
    params: { unit: app.service }
    check:
      active_state: active
      restarts: { lt: 3 }

  # daily backup timer fires and the backup succeeds
  - name: backup
    module: systemd
    params: { unit: backup.timer }
    check:
      active_state: active
      idle_age: { lt: 25h }
      service_result: success

  # a property without its own field
  - name: app-memory
    module: systemd
    params: { unit: app.service, properties: [MemoryCurrent] }
    check:
      properties.MemoryCurrent: { lt: 1073741824 }
```

`""` in `telnet-off` covers a unit that is not installed at all.
`properties.MemoryCurrent` is a number (bytes), so `lt` works on it; it is
`[not set]` when memory accounting is off, and `lt` then fails with "not
applicable to a string". Numbers beyond the int64 range
(`18446744073709551615`, systemd's "unlimited") stay text.

A failure names the rule and the value:

```
FAIL   backup   (systemd, 12ms)
       service_result: expected equals "success", got "exit-code"
```

---

# Output and results
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/output-and-results

A run reports its outcome in four places:

| Where | What | For |
|---|---|---|
| exit code | did everything pass | cron, systemd, scripts |
| stdout | every rule, or only the failing ones; text or JSON | people, pipelines |
| `<paths.results>/<name>/<rule>.json` | the latest result of each rule | dashboards, other tools |
| `<paths.events>/` | changes of state | notifications, see [State and events](/state-and-events) |

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | every rule that ran passed (also when there were no rules to run) |
| `1` | at least one rule has status `fail` or `error` |
| `2` | onecheck could not do its job: no or invalid config, unknown flag, another run of the same config in progress, results or events could not be written, the run was interrupted (SIGINT, SIGTERM) |

The exit code follows the status of **this run**, not the confirmed state: a
rule with `fail_after: 3` that failed once already gives `1`.

With code `2` nothing is printed on stdout; the reason is on stderr, prefixed
with `onecheck:`.

An interrupted run (Ctrl-C, `systemctl stop`, shutdown) kills the running
modules together with everything they started and records nothing: no
results, no state changes, no events. A half-finished check says nothing
about what it was checking, so it must not produce a `fail` event.

## Flags

```
onecheck run [-c <config>] [-o text|json] [--only-failed] [--rule <name>]... [--tag <tag>]...
```

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-o, --output text\|json` | output format, default `text` |
| `--only-failed` | list only rules with status `fail` or `error`; the summary still counts all rules |
| `--rule <name>` | run only this rule; repeatable |
| `--tag <tag>` | run only rules carrying this tag; repeatable |
| `--log-level <level>` | override `log.level` for this run and also print the log at that level on stderr |

With both `--rule` and `--tag`, a rule runs if it matches either. Disabled
rules (`enabled: false`) never run.

Results are printed on stdout only. Log lines never go to stdout, so
`onecheck -o json | jq` is safe; warnings and errors of onecheck itself go to
stderr and to the log file.

## Text output

```
PASS   passwd-sane   (file, 2ms)
FAIL   disk-usage    (command, 14ms)  [state: pass, 1/3]
       stdout: expected matches "^[0-7]\\d?%", got "91%\n"
FAIL   api-health    (http, 124ms)  [transition: fail]
       body json status: expected equals "ok", got "degraded"
       body json /checks/1/state: schema violation: value must be 'ok'
ERROR  cache-ping    (redis, 0ms)
       module "redis" is not installed in /usr/lib/onecheck/modules (see: onecheck module install --help)

4 rules: 1 passed, 2 failed, 1 errors
```

One line per rule: status, rule name, module and duration. Under a failing
rule, one line per condition that did not hold; under an `error`, the reason.

The note in brackets appears when the confirmed state needs explaining:

| Note | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `[transition: fail]` | this run changed the state to `fail`; an event was written |
| `[transition: recovered]` | this run changed the state back to `pass`; an event was written |
| `[transition: reminder]` | the state is still `fail` and `remind_every` has passed; a reminder event was written |
| `[state: pass, 1/3]` | the run did not pass, but the state is still `pass`: 1 of `fail_after: 3` |
| `[state: fail, 1/2]` | the run passed, but the state is still `fail`: 1 of `pass_after: 2` |

## JSON output

```sh
onecheck -o json
onecheck -o json --only-failed
```

```json
{
  "summary": { "total": 4, "passed": 1, "failed": 2, "errors": 1 },
  "results": [
    { "config": "main", "rule": "passwd-sane", "status": "pass", "...": "..." }
  ]
}
```

`summary` always counts every rule that ran. `results` lists them in config
order; with `--only-failed` it contains only the non-passing ones (possibly
`[]`). Each element has the [result format](#result-format) below.

```sh
# names of everything that is not fine
onecheck -o json | jq -r '.results[] | select(.status != "pass") | .rule'

# all failure messages
onecheck -o json --only-failed | jq -r '.results[] | .rule as $r | (.failures[].message, .error // empty) | "\($r): \(.)"'
```

## Result files

After every run each rule's result is stored at

```
<paths.results>/<config name>/<rule>.json
```

Passing and failing rules alike. There is no history: the file is replaced on
each run (atomically, so a reader never sees a half-written file). The
directory therefore always shows the current picture of all rules of a config.

Results of rules that were removed from the config or disabled are deleted by
the next full run (one without `--rule` / `--tag`).

## Result format

The same object is used in JSON output, in result files and inside events.

```json
{
  "config": "main",
  "rule": "api-health",
  "module": "http",
  "module_version": "1.2.0",
  "tags": ["api"],
  "status": "fail",
  "state": "pass",
  "transition": null,
  "consecutive": 2,
  "fail_after": 3,
  "pass_after": 2,
  "started_at": "2026-11-23T10:00:00.123Z",
  "duration_ms": 124,
  "failures": [
    {
      "path": "body",
      "json_path": "status",
      "operator": "equals",
      "expected": "ok",
      "actual": "degraded",
      "message": "body json status: expected equals \"ok\", got \"degraded\"",
      "fields": [
        { "path": "body", "json_path": "status", "operator": "equals", "actual": "degraded" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "error": null,
  "output": {
    "body": "{\"status\":\"degraded\",\"db\":\"timeout\"}",
    "headers": { "content-type": "application/json", "server": "nginx" }
  }
}
```

| Key | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `config` | string | `name` of the config |
| `rule` | string | rule name |
| `module` | string | module name |
| `module_version` | string | version of the module that ran; empty if the module could not be loaded |
| `tags` | array | the rule's tags, `[]` if none |
| `status` | string | outcome of this run: `pass`, `fail`, `error` |
| `state` | string | confirmed state after this run: `pass`, `fail` |
| `transition` | string or null | the event this run wrote: `fail` or `recovered` if it changed the state, `reminder` if the rule stays failed and a [reminder](/state-and-events#reminders) was due; else `null` |
| `consecutive` | number | how many runs in a row ended like this one (passing, or not passing) |
| `fail_after`, `pass_after` | number | the rule's thresholds |
| `started_at` | string | start of the check, UTC, RFC 3339 |
| `duration_ms` | number | how long the check took |
| `failures` | array | conditions that did not hold; `[]` unless `status` is `fail` |
| `error` | string or null | why the check could not run; set only when `status` is `error` |
| `output` | object | what the module saw, kept for diagnosis; `{}` if the module has no output fields or `output_tail` is `0`. See [Saved output](#saved-output) |

Each element of `failures`:

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `path` | the key of `check` the condition belongs to, e.g. `body`, `headers.content-type` |
| `json_path` | location inside a parsed JSON document, for `json.assert` (GJSON path) and `json.schema` (JSON pointer); absent otherwise |
| `operator` | the operator that did not hold, e.g. `equals`, `length gt`, `any`, `not`, `json`, `schema` |
| `expected` | the operator's argument from the config |
| `actual` | the value found; `null` if the path was missing; long values are cut to about 1 KB |
| `message` | a ready-to-show sentence combining the above |
| `fields` | a short list of the concrete fields behind the failure, see [Failed fields](#failed-fields); never empty for a failure onecheck writes |

### Failed fields

`message` is complete but can be long: for `any`, `not` and `some` it shows
the whole element and the whole condition. `fields` names only the concrete
leaf fields that decided the failure, with their values, so a notification
can say briefly what is wrong. Each element:

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `path` | full path to the field, including the element index, e.g. `containers.#(state=="running")#.2.name` |
| `json_path` | location inside a parsed JSON document, as in the failure; absent otherwise |
| `operator` | the operator applied to this field, e.g. `in`, `equals`, `length gt`, `exists` |
| `actual` | the field's value, cut like `actual` of the failure; `null` if the field is missing |
| `missing` | `true` when the field is absent; absent otherwise |

What the list holds:

| Failure | `fields` |
|---|---|
| a plain operator (`equals`, `in`, `length gt`, `exists`, `json`, `schema`, ...) | the field itself |
| `every` | one failure per failing element and condition, each with its own field |
| `any` | the failing fields of all the alternatives |
| `not` | the fields the negated condition checked and that held; a missing field has `missing: true` |
| `some` | the failing fields of every element |
| `every`/`some` on a path that is missing or not an array | the path itself |

A field that repeats (same `path`, `json_path` and `operator`) is listed
once, and the list stops at 20 entries. For example, this rule

```yaml
check:
  containers.#(state=="running")#:
    every:
      any:
        - { path: name, in: ["app-bot-1", "app-postgres-1"] }
```

writes, for every extra running container, a failure whose `message` shows
the whole container and whose `fields` names just the one that matters:

```json
"fields": [
  { "path": "containers.#(state==\"running\")#.2.name", "operator": "in", "actual": "smoke-tls-proxy" }
]
```

## Saved output

A failed `exit_code: 0` alone does not say what went wrong. So onecheck keeps
the raw output of the check in the result, **whether or not a condition uses
it and whether the rule passed or failed**:

| Module | Saved fields |
|---|---|
| `command` | `stdout`, `stderr` |
| `http` | `body`, `headers` |
| `file` | nothing |

Which fields are saved is decided by the module (it marks them as output, see
[Module protocol](/module-protocol)); how much is kept is decided by the
config:

```yaml
defaults:
  output_tail: 10k      # default for every rule; this is also the built-in default

rules:
  - name: backup
    module: command
    output_tail: 100k   # more for this rule
    params: { run: /opt/backup/run.sh }
    check: { exit_code: 0 }

  - name: token-check
    module: http
    output_tail: 0      # keep nothing: the response holds secrets
    params: { url: https://example.com/token }
    check: { status: 200 }
```

- The size is per field and accepts `k`, `m` (`1k`, `10k`, `1m`) as well as
  `KB`, `MB`; a bare number is bytes.
- A longer text is cut to its **last** `output_tail` bytes and then starts
  with `…`: the end of the output is where the error usually is.
- A value that is not text (`headers`) is kept whole if it fits into
  `output_tail` and left out otherwise.
- A command killed by its `timeout` still has the output it printed before
  that in `output`, next to `status: error`.
- Output is cut from what the module returned, which is itself limited by
  `run.max_field_size` (default `10MB`): of a larger output only the first
  `max_field_size` bytes are seen at all.

The result file is overwritten by the next run, so `output` always belongs to
the latest run. An [event](/state-and-events) embeds the result of the run
that changed the state, including its `output`, so a notification can show
why the check failed.

Saved output may contain secrets (tokens in a response body, passwords
printed by a script). Result directories are created with mode `0750` and
files with `0640`; set `output_tail: 0` on rules whose output must not be
stored.

---

# State and events
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/onecheck/state-and-events

onecheck does not only tell whether a check passes right now. For every rule
it keeps a **confirmed state** between runs and records each change of that
state as an **event**. This is what a notification service builds on: it gets
told when something broke and when it recovered, once per change, and is
reminded while the problem stays, regardless of which module the rule uses.

[onenotify](https://alekzonder.github.io/onenotify) is such a service: it
takes the events described here and delivers them to Telegram, mail or ntfy.
onecheck itself sends nothing.

## Status and state

Two different things are reported for each rule:

| | Values | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `status` | `pass`, `fail`, `error` | the outcome of **this run** |
| `state` | `pass`, `fail` | the **confirmed** state, which changes only after enough runs in a row |

`status` values:

- `pass` — every condition held;
- `fail` — at least one condition did not hold;
- `error` — the check could not be carried out: module missing or
  incompatible, invalid rule, timeout, no connection, value too large.

For the state, `error` counts the same as `fail`: a check that cannot run is
not known to be healthy. The distinction stays visible in `status`.

## Thresholds: `fail_after`, `pass_after`

```yaml
rules:
  - name: api-health
    module: http
    fail_after: 3     # 3 non-passing runs in a row → state becomes fail
    pass_after: 2     # 2 passing runs in a row → state becomes pass again
    params: { url: https://example.com/health }
    check: { status: 200 }
```

Both default to `1` (from `defaults` in the config), which means the state
follows the status immediately.

The rules:

- In state `pass`, after `fail_after` consecutive runs that did not pass, the
  state becomes `fail`.
- In state `fail`, after `pass_after` consecutive passing runs, the state
  becomes `pass`.
- A run with the opposite outcome resets the count.
- A rule seen for the first time starts in state `pass` without an event. If
  it is failing, it goes to `fail` through the normal `fail_after` rule.

Example with `fail_after: 3`, `pass_after: 2`:

| Run | status | consecutive | state | event |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | pass | 1 | pass | |
| 2 | fail | 1 | pass | |
| 3 | fail | 2 | pass | |
| 4 | pass | 1 | pass | (count reset) |
| 5 | fail | 1 | pass | |
| 6 | fail | 2 | pass | |
| 7 | fail | 3 | **fail** | `fail` |
| 8 | fail | 4 | fail | |
| 9 | pass | 1 | fail | |
| 10 | pass | 2 | **pass** | `recovered` |

Thresholds count **runs**, not time: with a cron line every minute,
`fail_after: 3` means roughly three minutes.

The process exit code and the printed output follow `status`, not `state`: a
rule that failed once with `fail_after: 3` already makes `onecheck` exit with
`1`. The text output shows the gap, e.g. `[state: pass, 1/3]`.

A manual `onecheck run --rule <name>` updates the state and writes events
exactly like a scheduled run.

## Reminders

A `fail` event is written once. If nobody fixed the problem, onecheck says so
again: while a rule's state stays `fail`, it writes a `reminder` event every
`remind_every`.

```yaml
defaults:
  remind_every: 60m     # the built-in default

rules:
  - name: api-health
    module: http
    remind_every: 15m   # this one more often
    params: { url: https://example.com/health }
    check: { status: 200 }

  - name: nightly-report
    module: file
    remind_every: 0     # one notification is enough: no reminders
    params: { path: /var/reports/today.csv }
    check: { exists: true }
```

- Reminders are on by default, every 60 minutes. `remind_every: 0` turns them
  off, for one rule or in `defaults` for all.
- Reminders are due at fixed times counted from the start of the problem:
  after `remind_every`, after twice that, and so on. A reminder is written by
  the first run after a due time, so a run that starts late does not shift
  the following ones. A run up to a tenth of `remind_every` early counts as
  on time: with `remind_every` equal to the interval the config is run at,
  every run of a failed rule writes a reminder.
- One run writes at most one reminder for a rule. After the host was down
  for a day there is one reminder, not twenty-four.
- A run that **passed** writes no reminder, even if the state is still `fail`
  because `pass_after` has not been reached. If the next run fails again, the
  reminder is written then.
- A run that ended with `error` is reminded of like any failing run.
- The reminder carries the result of the run that wrote it, so the
  notification shows the problem as it is now, and `since`: when it began.

onecheck has no scheduler, so a reminder cannot come more often than the
config is run. A `remind_every` shorter than the time since the rule's
previous run means "on every run"; onecheck then logs a warning:

```
level=WARN msg="remind_every is shorter than the time between runs, a reminder is written on every run" rule=api-health remind_every=1m0s since_last_run=5m0s
```

Raise `remind_every` or run the config more often. The warning is given only
for a value set in the config, not for the built-in 60 minutes of a config
that runs once a day. After the host was down, one such warning is expected.

## Events

Every change of a rule's confirmed state, and every
[reminder](#reminders), writes one file into the event queue directory,
`paths.events`:

```
/var/lib/onecheck/events/20261123T100200Z-main-api-health-fail.json
```

The file name is the event id: `<UTC time>-<config name>-<rule>-<transition>`.

```json
{
  "id": "20261123T100200Z-main-api-health-fail",
  "config": "main",
  "rule": "api-health",
  "transition": "fail",
  "from": "pass",
  "to": "fail",
  "at": "2026-11-23T10:02:00Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-24T10:02:00Z",
  "since": "2026-11-23T10:02:00Z",
  "params": {
    "url": "https://example.com/health",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${API_TOKEN}" }
  },
  "redacted": false,
  "output_fields": [],
  "result": {
    "config": "main",
    "rule": "api-health",
    "module": "http",
    "module_version": "1.2.0",
    "tags": ["api"],
    "status": "fail",
    "state": "fail",
    "transition": "fail",
    "consecutive": 3,
    "fail_after": 3,
    "pass_after": 2,
    "started_at": "2026-11-23T10:01:59.874Z",
    "duration_ms": 124,
    "failures": [
      {
        "path": "status",
        "operator": "equals",
        "expected": 200,
        "actual": 503,
        "message": "status: expected equals 200, got 503",
        "fields": [
          { "path": "status", "operator": "equals", "actual": 503 }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "error": null,
    "output": {
      "body": "upstream connect error",
      "headers": { "content-type": "text/plain" }
    }
  }
}
```

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `id` | unique id, equal to the file name without `.json` |
| `config` | `name` of the config the rule belongs to |
| `rule` | rule name |
| `transition` | `fail` (pass → fail), `recovered` (fail → pass) or `reminder` (still fail) |
| `from`, `to` | confirmed state before and after; both `fail` for a reminder |
| `at` | when the event was recorded (UTC, RFC 3339) |
| `expires_at` | `at` + `events.ttl`; after this the event may be deleted |
| `since` | when the state in `to` began: equal to `at` for `fail` and `recovered`, the time of the `fail` event for a reminder |
| `params` | the rule's `params` exactly as written in the config, before `${VAR}` is replaced; `null` when the rule has none or has `event_params: false` |
| `redacted` | `true` when the rule has `event_params: false`: a consumer must not show the details of this event (params, failures, error) to third parties |
| `output_fields` | names of the keys of `result.output` the rule allows a notification to show, from the rule's [`event_output`](#output-in-notifications); `[]` unless the rule says otherwise, and always `[]` with `event_params: false` |
| `result` | the full result of the run that wrote the event, see [Output and results](/output-and-results#result-format) |

For a `recovered` event, `result` is the passing run (`failures` is empty).
For a `fail` event caused by a check that could not run, `result.status` is
`error` and `result.error` holds the reason.

A reminder is the same file with `reminder` in its name and `since` pointing
back to the start of the problem (`result` is left out here):

```json
{
  "id": "20261123T110215Z-main-api-health-reminder",
  "config": "main",
  "rule": "api-health",
  "transition": "reminder",
  "from": "fail",
  "to": "fail",
  "at": "2026-11-23T11:02:15Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-24T11:02:15Z",
  "since": "2026-11-23T10:02:00Z",
  "params": { "url": "https://example.com/health" },
  "redacted": false,
  "output_fields": [],
  "result": { "status": "fail", "state": "fail", "transition": "reminder", "consecutive": 63 }
}
```

### What an event can reveal

An event is meant to be turned into a notification, which usually leaves the
host: a chat, a mail, a push service. Two parts of it deserve a look.

**Params.** `params` holds what the config file says, not what the module
received. A secret passed as `${VAR}` stays `${VAR}`:

```yaml
params:
  url: https://example.com/health
  headers: { Authorization: "Bearer ${API_TOKEN}" }   # the event says ${API_TOKEN}
```

A secret typed into the config as plain text is copied into the event as it
is. Use `${VAR}`, see
[Configuration](/configuration#environment-variables-in-params).

**Failures and errors.** A failure message names the value that was found:
`body: expected contains "ok", got "<the first 1024 bytes of the body>"`. A
condition on a response body or on a command's output therefore puts a piece
of that body or output into the event. `result.output` holds its tail as
well, see [Output and results](/output-and-results#saved-output). A
notification shows saved output only for the fields a rule names in
[`event_output`](#output-in-notifications).

To keep a rule's details out of notifications, set `event_params: false`:

```yaml
rules:
  - name: token-check
    module: http
    event_params: false   # the event has "params": null and "redacted": true
    output_tail: 0        # and no saved output
    params: { url: https://example.com/token }
    check: { status: 200 }
```

The event is still written, with its full `result`: `redacted` is an
instruction to the consumer. onenotify then sends only the rule name, the
module, the tags and the time. `event_params` can be set for all rules in
`defaults`.

### Output in notifications

`result.output` holds what the module saw: a command's stdout and stderr, a
response body and headers. It is in every event, but a notification does not
show it: output can contain anything. A rule whose output is safe and useful
to read says which part may be shown:

```yaml
rules:
  - name: backup
    module: command
    event_output: [stderr]      # a notification may show stderr, not stdout
    params: { run: /usr/local/bin/backup.sh }
    check: { exit_code: 0 }
```

The event then has `"output_fields": ["stderr"]`. This is only a mark for
the consumer: the event's `result.output` is the same with or without it.

- Only output fields of the rule's module can be named: `stdout` and
  `stderr` for `command`, `body` and `headers` for `http`. Another name, or
  any name for a module without output fields, makes the rule an `error`.
- The default is to show nothing. `event_output` is a key of a rule; there is
  none in `defaults`, because output fields differ between modules.
- `event_params: false` is stronger: the event has `"output_fields": []`.
- How much output exists is still decided by `output_tail`, see
  [Output and results](/output-and-results#saved-output). With
  `output_tail: 0` there is nothing to show.

### Consuming the queue

The queue is a plain directory, shared by all configs on the host. The
contract for a consumer (the notification service):

1. List `*.json` files. Files are written atomically (temp file + rename), so
   a visible `.json` file is always complete. Ignore names starting with `.`.
2. Process the event.
3. Delete the file.

Ordering: file names start with a UTC timestamp, so a lexicographic sort is
chronological.

Delivery is at-least-once: if a consumer crashes between processing and
deleting, it will see the event again. Use `id` to deduplicate.

Events nobody consumed are removed by `onecheck logrotate` once `expires_at`
has passed (`events.ttl`, default `24h`). See
[Logging and logrotate](/logging-and-logrotate).

### No lost transitions

For each rule onecheck writes the event first and the new state after it. If
the event cannot be written (disk full, no permission), the state is left
unchanged and the run ends with exit code `2`; the next run detects the same
change again and retries. A change of state is therefore either in the queue
or reported as a failed run, never silently dropped.

Reminders follow the same order. If the state cannot be saved after a
reminder was written, the next run writes that reminder once more: a
consumer may see a duplicate, never a gap.

## Files

| Path | Content | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| `<paths.state>/<name>/<rule>.json` | confirmed state, consecutive counters, time of the last reminder and of the previous run | internal, do not edit |
| `<paths.state>/<name>/.lock`, `.owner` | run lock; which config file owns the name | internal |
| `<paths.results>/<name>/<rule>.json` | latest result of the rule | overwritten every run |
| `<paths.events>/<id>.json` | one state change or reminder | until consumed or expired |

State and result files of a rule that was removed from the config (or
disabled) are deleted by the next full run, that is a run without `--rule` or
`--tag`. A state file that cannot be read is logged as a warning and the rule
is treated as new.

Renaming a rule starts it from scratch: the state is keyed by rule name.
Changing a rule's module or conditions keeps its state.
